In Genesis 49:6, Jacob reproaches the sons of Simeon and Levi: "in their wickedness, they have cut the hocks of the bulls," showing that it is a violent act committed out of rage.
2. In war, cutting the hock of a horse prevents it from fighting. After each military victory, Israelite generals apply this practice: Joshua "cut the hocks of their horses" (Joshua 11:9), just as David did after defeating the enemy (2 Samuel 8:4). It is a strategy to neutralize the military power of the opponent by rendering their animal armament unusable.
3. Figuratively, the action evokes the systematic destruction of an enemy's ability to harm: it is not about killing, but about disabling, rendering harmless and dependent.
H6131B.origine: The Hebrew word עִקֵּר (iqquér) is formed from a root that fundamentally means "to cut" or "to sever." The verb is in the Piel (intensive form in Hebrew), which emphasizes the deliberate and repeated action of mutilation. The root conjures the image of weaning, detaching, isolating a part from the whole, applied here to a military and brutal action.
H6131B.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, always to describe the "cutting of hocks" of military animals. In Genesis 49:6, Jacob mentions it as an act of cruelty committed by his sons. From Joshua and in the accounts of David, it is an established military strategy after victory: the enemy's horses are paralyzed to prevent them from regrouping militarily. The four occurrences related to wars (Joshua 11:6, 11:9; 2 Samuel 8:4; 1 Chronicles 18:4) depict commands or executions of divine or royal order, while the first (Genesis 49:6) presents it as a condemned violence.
H6131B.portee: This word reminds us that military victory in Israel was not limited to killing the enemy, but to destroying their future capacity to harm: an ancient form of disarmament. It also testifies to the raw reality of ancient warfare, without idealization. For the believer, it can evoke how God neutralizes the powers that oppose Him — not through blind destruction, but by rendering them powerless to continue their rebellion.

sens: Remove a plant from the ground by pulling its roots
Destroy or completely make disappear
Uproot, forcibly remove
H6132.detail: 1. The primary and concrete meaning is that of a plant being pulled from the ground to completely uproot it: it is the work of uprooting weeds or roots. In Daniel 7:8, three horns are "uprooted" before a new horn: the image is that of something established and rooted being forcibly removed, as one uproots a plant. 2. Figuratively, the word expresses the idea of total destruction or violent disappearance: it is not a simple withdrawal, but a complete removal, as if one wanted no trace to remain. The three uprooted horns symbolize kingdoms or powers completely erased. 3. The word can also mean "to extirpate" or "to forcibly remove," in the sense of taking something out of its context or established power: it is thus a violent and definitive action.
H6132.origine: The Hebrew verb עֲקַר (aqar) comes from a root that evokes the idea of depriving oneself of something anchored or established. The word is rarely used in the Old Testament, and it always carries this force of total uprooting. The root itself suggests an action of rupture with what was fixed and stable.
H6132.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 7:8, at the heart of a prophetic vision where the prophet sees royal horns. In this context of apocalyptic revelation, the three uprooted horns represent kingdoms or powers that disappear before a new dominant power. The unique use of the word enhances the dramatic effect: it is a definitive and spectacular action, worthy of the heavenly vision that Daniel contemplates.
H6132.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that certain powers or human authorities, as powerful as they may seem, can be removed by the will of God. The image of uprooting shows a destruction that is not gradual but total and irrevocable: it invites us not to place our trust in earthly kingdoms that pass away, but in the divine authority that endures.

sens: child or descendant
member of a family lineage
someone from the kinship
H6133.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a child or a descendant — literally a branch that grows from the trunk of a family. In Leviticus 25:47, it refers to "someone from the family of the foreigner," meaning a relative, a child, or a close person of the master of the poor who comes to sell himself: the text mentions members of the same household capable of redeeming a poor person who has become a slave.
2. More broadly, the word designates any member of a lineage, anyone who belongs to the family by blood or by covenant — someone who counts in the continuity of the clan or household.
H6133.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "root" or "foundation" (see עִקַּר, "root"). Just as a root produces branches and shoots, the word עֵקֶר designates what grows and extends from a source — a descendant or offspring. It is a natural image: from the family root come the branches that are the children and the following generations.
H6133.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Leviticus 25:47. It concerns a law about slavery and freedom: if a poor Israelite must sell himself due to debts, he can be redeemed by a close relative of the foreign master — that is, "someone from the family of the foreigner." The context shows that the word applies to any kinship link capable of creating a redemption obligation, emphasizing the family duty in the Torah.
H6133.portee: This word reminds us that in biblical thought, no one is isolated: each person belongs to a lineage, to a family that shares duties and solidarity. The law of redemption stated in Leviticus 25 shows that the family has responsibilities towards its own — including towards the poor and the slave. For the Christian, it is an invitation to recognize one's ties with the community of believers and the moral obligations that arise from them.

sens: Man from the tribe of Judah, brother of Maats and Jamin
H6134.detail: Eker is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogy of Judah. He is the son of Ram and the brother of Maats and Jamin (1 Chronicles 2:27). His name appears in the list of descendants of Jerachmeel, who was himself the son of Hezron and grandson of Judah. This Eker lived during the time of the divided monarchy, but the Bible gives us the bare minimum about him: his name, his father, and his brothers. There is no account of his deeds or life.
H6134.origine: The name Eker literally means "offspring" or "descendant" in Hebrew, evoking the image of a young shoot that grows. This meaning fits a character known primarily for belonging to a long genealogical chain of descendants of Judah. The name itself reminds us that each generation is a new "offspring" of the previous one.
H6134.emploi: Eker appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:27, in the genealogical record of the descendants of Judah. He is listed among the three sons of Ram: Maats, Jamin, and Eker. These genealogies in 1 Chronicles aim to establish the lineages of God's people after the exile, showing the continuity of the promised descent to Judah. Although Eker is known by his name alone, his inclusion in this genealogy places him among the authentic families of Israel.

sens: Unable to bear children
Not yielding fruit or harvest
Empty, unproductive, without result
H6135.detail:
1. The most common meaning concerns a woman unable to conceive. When the Bible states that a woman is barren, it means she cannot conceive. This is what we read about Sarai in Genesis 11:30 ("Sarai was barren; she had no children") or about Rachel in Genesis 29:31. Barrenness was experienced as suffering and shame in the Old Testament, as giving life was the expected role of a woman, and the promise of offspring was at the heart of divine covenants.
2. The word extends to any creature or thing that produces nothing: Job 24:21 applies it to the "barren" animals of the flock, and Deuteronomy 7:14 promises that there will be "no man or woman barren, nor any barren animal" among the people of Israel. It conveys the general idea of a lack of fertility, an absence of yield.
3. In a figurative or spiritual sense, the word can evoke anything that is empty of meaning or without lasting result — although this latter sense is less explicit in the provided usages. The emphasis remains on the inability to produce, to generate, to grow.
H6135.origine: The Hebrew word עָקָר (aqar) comes from a root that evokes the idea of "uprooting" or "pulling out" — hence its connection with barrenness, as if life were "pulled away" or blocked before it could sprout and grow. The same root appears in other Hebrew words concerning infertility. When translating the Old Testament into Greek, translators often used the Greek word στεῖρα (steira) to convey this concept.
H6135.emploi: This word appears 11 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the Pentateuch and the narratives of the judges. It primarily applies to women: Sarai, Rebecca, Rachel, the mother of Samson (Genesis and Judges) — all major figures through whom God miraculously brought forth offspring, showing that barrenness in Israel was often the ground for divine intervention. It is also used for the animals of the flock (Deuteronomy 7:14) and for the promises of fertility for the entire people (Exodus 23:26). The scope thus extends from the individual to the community: it is a key word in the narratives of promise and divine blessing.
H6135.portee: For the Christian reader, barrenness in the Bible is never a definitive curse, but often the starting point of a miraculous intervention by God. The barren women of the Old Testament — Sarai, Rebecca, Rachel, the mother of Samson — all bore children against all odds, signaling that God alone controls life and can do what seems impossible. This theme also reveals that divine blessing comes through the child, the offspring, the continuity of the covenant: bringing forth a people from a barren woman affirms that God's plan is stronger than our limitations. It is a school of faith.

sens: Lower part of a tree, that which remains after the branches are cut off
Foundation or stable base of something
That which persists and can regenerate despite destruction
H6136.detail:
1. The trunk is the thick, lower part of a tree, that which remains rooted in the ground when the branches and foliage are cut away. In Daniel's vision, the king of Babylon sees a great tree cut down, but he is commanded to leave the "trunk where the roots are" (Daniel 4:15), so that life can continue to nourish the tree from its underground base.

2. By extension, the trunk refers to what is fundamental and stable, that which remains when all that is visible or superficial collapses. When the interpretation of the dream explains "the trunk where the roots of the tree are," it signifies that the king's kingdom will remain with him, that his royalty will have a permanent base (Daniel 4:26), even if everything seems destroyed.

3. This is why the trunk symbolizes what can regenerate, what is capable of sprouting again. Although rooted and immobile, it carries within it the power of life; it does not die, but waits for the moment of its restoration.
H6136.origine: This Aramaic word is close to the Hebrew עֵקֶר (éqer, "descendant" or "offspring"), which shares the same root. The root evokes the idea of what is firm and established, of what takes root. The trunk is therefore the natural image of stability, of underground continuity, of what remains when everything else is gone.
H6136.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, all in the book of Daniel (4:15, 4:23, 4:26), in the context of a royal vision. Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a great tree cut down by a heavenly command, but whose rooted trunk must be left. The same passage is repeated twice (the dream itself, then its repetition), and the prophetic interpretation explains what the trunk means: the promise that the kingdom will return to the king after his temporary fall. The word is used strictly concretely (a part of a tree) to serve a spiritual lesson about restoration.
H6136.portee: This image of the trunk that remains when the tree is cut down teaches a comforting truth: even when God humbles or brings low a man, even when all that appears great collapses, the base, the root, the true foundation can remain. For the Christian reader, it speaks of God's faithfulness to His promise, and of the always-open possibility of restoration and new rooting in His grace.

sens: Venomous creature of the desert, resembling a crab with a curved tail ending in a stinger
Instrument of punishment equipped with spikes or cords, used for whipping
Hostile creature or surrounding threat
H6137.detail:
1. The scorpion is a dangerous creature from the Arabian desert, feared for its deadly venom. The Bible mentions it among the natural perils that the Hebrews faced in the desert: in Deuteronomy 8:15, it symbolizes the terrors of the journey to the promised land, alongside fiery serpents.
2. The word takes on a figurative meaning when it designates a whip equipped with spikes or blades — an instrument of torture much crueler than a simple whip. Rehoboam threatens to use "scorpions" to punish the people, far worse than his father's ordinary whip (1 Kings 12:11, 12:14).
3. More broadly, the scorpion represents a threat, a hostile danger or surrounding hostility. Ezekiel, sent to prophesy among the rebels of Israel, is surrounded by "thorns, thistles, and scorpions" — images of the malice and hostility he must face (Ezekiel 2:6).
H6137.origine: The Hebrew word עַקְרָב (aqrav) derives from a root that evokes a point or stinger: the name literally means "the one who stings." In Aramaic and Arabic, similar words retain this idea. The image remains that of the feared creature of the Near Eastern desert, with its venomous stinger: this is why the word has naturally extended to any sharp and painful instrument, notably the whip equipped with spikes.
H6137.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the same form, in three different contexts. First, it designates the real animal of the desert (Deuteronomy 8:15). Then, it takes on the figurative meaning of a torture instrument: Rehoboam, wanting to show his firmness, threatens to punish the people "with scorpions" instead of his father's simple whip — this passage appears four times, repeated in 1 Kings 12:11 and 12:14, then in 2 Chronicles 10:11 and 10:14. Finally, Ezekiel uses "scorpions" to evoke the hostility that surrounds him. The meaning thus shifts from the real to the metaphorical, from the concrete animal to the idea of threat or cruel punishment.
H6137.portee: The scorpion reminds us that faith goes through concrete trials: the desert, with its perils, tests trust in God and makes us recognize His help. The "scorpion" whip warns of the danger of tyrannical pride — Rehoboam, disregarding the advice of the elders, incurs a punishment far worse than what he threatens: the division of the kingdom. And for the prophet, the "scorpions" signify that serving God in a hostile world does not eliminate hostility, but gives the strength to move forward without fear.

sens: Fortified city of the Philistines in Canaan
Stronghold in the northern part of Philistine territory
Idolatrous city associated with Baal-Zebub
H6138.detail:
1. Ekron is one of the five major Philistine cities in Canaan, located in the coastal and hilly region to the north of these pagan peoples' territory. It notably appears in the enumeration of Israel's borders (Joshua 13:3) and the conquered cities (Joshua 15:46), marking the limits of the Canaanite territory before Israel took possession of the land.

2. It is an important stronghold in northern Philistia, governed by a prince like the other major cities in the block (Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath). It holds strategic importance in the confrontation between Israel and the Philistines: after Samuel's victory at Mizpah, the cities from Gaza to Ekron "returned to Israel" (1 Samuel 7:14), marking a turning point in the domination of the territory.

3. Ekron is the seat of worship for Baal-Zebub, the god of flies and a major pagan deity among the Philistines. When King Ahaziah of Samaria asks his messengers to consult this god, Elijah intervenes to redirect them to the Lord (2 Kings 1:2-3), reminding that only the true God of Israel is the source of knowledge and life.
H6138.origine: The name etymologically means "emigration" or "uprooting," perhaps evoking the distant origins of the Philistines, a people that came from the sea. Ekron is a historically attested city through archaeology and Assyrian inscriptions. Its political and religious importance makes it a key site in the Canaanite world and an essential geographical landmark in the Old Testament.
H6138.emploi: Ekron appears about twenty times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of Joshua, 1 Samuel, and 2 Kings. It is mentioned during the delimitation of the lands (Joshua 13:3, 15:46), in Israel's military campaigns against the Philistines (1 Samuel 5:10, 7:14, 17:52), and as a center of the idolatrous worship of Baal-Zebub (2 Kings 1:3). The prophets (Jeremiah, Amos, Zephaniah, Zechariah) include it in their oracles of judgment against the nations, testifying to its persistence as a stronghold of paganism until the end of the Old Testament era.
H6138.portee: Ekron symbolizes in the Bible the earthly power of the pagan world, opaque to the truth of God and closed to His authority. Its mention reminds believers that even the great human fortifications and the gods of the nations do not withstand the will of the true God and His plans for salvation. The contrast between the idolatry of Baal-Zebub and the power of the Lord guiding Elijah teaches that consulting false gods is vain and that only the God of Israel deserves trust.

sens: Philistine city in Palestine
One of the five major cities of the Philistines
H6139.detail: 1. Ekron is an important city in the territory of the Philistines, located in the northern part of their domain (Joshua 13:3). It is one of the five major centers of Philistine power, each governed by a prince: Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron. 2. It is a strategic and prestigious location in the political geography of ancient Canaan, where the Philistines exercised their political and military control before the Israelite conquest.
H6139.origine: The name "Ekron" comes from the Hebrew עֶקְרוֹן (eqrôn), whose etymology may refer to an idea of "migration" or "transplantation," images that perhaps evoke the distant history of this people. The adjective עֶקְרוֹנִי (eqronî) simply designates an inhabitant or something belonging to Ekron, according to the usual model of forming adjectives and ethnic terms in Hebrew.
H6139.emploi: Ekron appears twice in the provided texts. In Joshua 13:3, it is named among the five Philistine capitals that are to be conquered during the possession of Canaan. In 1 Samuel 5:10, it reappears in the context of the captured Ark of the Covenant by the Philistines, showing its central role in the political and religious affairs of the Philistine country. The city remains a major landmark of the land borders and military stakes of the time.

sens: that deviates from the straight line, that strays from the direct path
that moves away from justice, integrity, and uprightness
that alters, distorts, or perverts what is just and good
that is recognized or declared guilty
H6140.detail:
1. The word first evokes a physical image: a path that winds, that strays from the direct trajectory. In Proverbs 10:9, one who "takes crooked paths" contrasts with one who "walks in integrity" — it is an image of detour, of voluntary deviation.
2. It then applies to morality and justice: a crooked action is a twisted action, contrary to what is right and honest. The leaders in Micah 3:9 "pervert all that is right," transforming justice into injustice.
3. The verb can also designate the act of twisting, of deliberately distorting: in Isaiah 59:8, the wicked "take crooked paths" that deliberately stray from the way of peace.
4. In Job 9:20, the word describes a verdict: my own mouth will declare me "guilty," that is, will recognize me as crooked, contrary to justice.
H6140.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of twisting, bending, deviating. It paints the image of a rope being twisted or a path that winds. The word belongs to a family of expressions of twisting, deviation, and perversity — it naturally opposes words for uprightness, integrity, and justice that recur throughout Proverbs.
H6140.emploi: The verb appears 5 times in the Old Testament, mainly in biblical wisdom (Proverbs and Job) and in the prophets. In Proverbs, it describes the corrupt paths that men choose: one who walks "in crooked ways" will be discovered (10:9) or will fall (28:18). In Job 9:20, it expresses the idea of being judged guilty. In Micah, it takes on a more serious moral meaning: the leaders "pervert" justice itself. In Isaiah 59:8, it depicts the paths of the wicked, far from peace. The word is always linked to a moral deviation: straying from uprightness means falling into wrongdoing, injustice, or lies.
H6140.portee: This word teaches that lies, injustice, and malice are not consequence-free detours: they are crooked paths that stray from peace and ultimately end up being discovered or condemned. For the Christian, it invites one to walk in uprightness and integrity, as the Israelite wisdom intended, rather than seeking crooked justifications or detours. It is a call to honesty and integrity before God and men.

sens: That is twisted, bent, not straight
That deviates from the straight path, that strays from good
That is false, deceptive, dishonest
That acts with malice, ill-intentioned
H6141.detail:
1. In a concrete sense, the word evokes something physically twisted or bent, that is not straight — like a path that winds and zigzags. In Proverbs 2:15, it speaks of those "who follow crooked paths, and who take twisted roads": the word literally designates these paths that do not go straight to the goal.
2. In a moral and religious sense, it is the deviation from the straight path of God. A perverse person voluntarily strays from what is just and good, turning away from uprightness. In Psalms 101:4, the psalmist rejects "the perverse heart": one who knowingly deviates from good.
3. The word also designates what is false or deceptive in speech and actions. In Proverbs 8:8, Wisdom asserts that her words "have nothing false or twisted": she is honest and true. This is the opposite of deception.
4. Finally, perverse describes the attitude of one who acts with intentional malice. In 2 Samuel 22:27, God declares, "with the perverse you act according to his perversity": one who acts badly will be treated according to that malice.
H6141.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to twist, to bend, to deviate." The basic image is physical: what is twisted is not in a straight line. From there, it extends to the moral idea: one who deviates from the straight way, who turns away from good. The word belongs to the family of biblical terms that oppose uprightness (what goes straight ahead) to perversity (what zigzags, what strays).
H6141.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Proverbs and Psalms. It designates sometimes perverse people ("the perverse"), sometimes their acts or their nature. In Deuteronomy 32:5, Moses reproaches the people for being a "crooked and perverse generation," led astray from God. In Proverbs, the word often returns to describe one who follows paths of evil: in Proverbs 11:20 and 17:20, it is one who has "a perverse heart." The biblical context shows that perversity is a deliberate refusal of wisdom and justice: it is never presented as an excusable weakness, but as a choice against God.
H6141.portee: This word reminds the reader that biblical morality is a matter of direction and choice. The perverse is not someone who has made an isolated mistake, but someone whose whole heart deviates from good: it is a voluntary distancing from God. Recognizing perversity for what it is — not a weakness, but a conscious deviation — helps the believer see their own responsibility and return to uprightness.

sens: father of Ira, mighty warrior of David
H6142.detail: Ikkesch is a man from the time of the united monarchy in Israel, known only as the father of Ira the Tekoite. Ira was one of the mighty warriors (or "mighty men") of King David, and he also commanded a military division of twenty-four thousand men in the sixth month of the year (1 Chronicles 27:9). The name "Ikkesch" means "twisted" or "perverse," perhaps an allusion to a physical trait or character, but the Bible provides no details about this man himself.
H6142.origine: The Hebrew name עִקֵּשׁ (Ikkesch) comes from a root that designates what is twisted, bent, or perverted. It is an uncommon name in the Old Testament and appears only to identify the father of Ira. The meaning of the name could reflect a personal trait, but the Bible never explains it.
H6142.emploi: Ikkesch appears only three times in the Bible, always as the father of Ira the Tekoite. He is first mentioned in 2 Samuel 23:26, in the list of David's mighty warriors, then in 1 Chronicles 11:28 with the same genealogy. Finally, in 1 Chronicles 27:9, his son Ira is named as the military chief responsible for the administration of the kingdom in the sixth month. These three passages show that Ikkesch's renown rests entirely on that of his son Ira, a trusted man of King David.

sens: Deviation, diversion from the right path
Lie, twisted or deceptive word
Intentional deception, malicious trickery
H6143.detail:
1. The word literally evokes something curved, deformed, like a path that strays from the straight line. This is the basic image: what is not straight. In Proverbs 4:24, we see this image applied to speech — "Put away from you a falsehood" means to reject the twisted word, the one that deviates from the truth.
2. By extension, it designates the lie itself: a word that distorts reality, that hides the truth under detours. The verse adds, "Remove from your lips the detours" to clarify: it is a word that circumvents the truth.
3. It is also a voluntary deception, a dishonest act. In Proverbs 6:12, the wicked man walks "with falsehood in his mouth" — meaning he deliberately lies, using trickery to deceive.
H6143.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be twisted, to be crooked." The central image is that of curvature, distortion: what is not straight, what deviates. Falsehood is therefore always presented in biblical Hebrew as a kind of deviation — a deviation from the truth, a word that strays from the right path of honesty.
H6143.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the book of Proverbs. Each time it refers to false or deceptive words: in Proverbs 4:24, the wise man invites to reject the falsehood of his mouth as one would guard against a disease; in Proverbs 6:12, falsehood is the characteristic trait of the wicked and perverse man, who constantly carries it in his mouth. The Book of Proverbs, which cultivates wisdom through contrasts, opposes falsehood to uprightness, sincerity, and truth.
H6143.portee: This word reminds the believer that lying is never trivial: it is a deviation from God's path, a corruption of the word that unites men. Biblical wisdom teaches that removing falsehood from one's mouth is to turn away from evil and walk straight toward good. It is a call to total sincerity in our words, reflecting our attachment to God's truth.

sens: City of Moab located south of the Arnon River
H6144.detail: Ar is a major Moabite city, likely the capital or a very important city of the kingdom of Moab, marking its northern border. It was located south of the Arnon River, which separated Moab from the lands the Israelites crossed during their exodus. It is a strategic site mentioned in the Bible during the Israelites' passage toward Canaan, and the prophets mention it among the cities that God's judgment will reach.
H6144.origine: The name Ar literally means "city" in ancient Hebrew: it is a generic term that became a proper name to designate this particular city of Moab. The name simply reflects its significant urban status in the region.
H6144.emploi: Ar appears six times in the Bible, always in connection with Moab and its borders. In the accounts of Deuteronomy (chapter 2), it marks the southern limit that the Israelites were not to exceed during their journey toward the Jordan: it is at Ar that they crossed the border of Moab without attacking it, at the command of the Lord. Later, the prophet Isaiah mentions it as a city destined for destruction, associated with Kir-Moab, in an oracle of judgment against Moab. The city embodied Moabite power and territorial stability.

sens: one who opposes someone, who wishes them harm
one who fights, who makes war
one who opposes God or His people
H6145.detail: 1. It is one who opposes a person, wishes them harm, or hates them. The enemy is by nature hostile: he conspires against you, speaks of you "in a criminal manner" (Psalms 139:20). 2. It is also one who fights in a military sense, who confronts someone in war or in duel. 3. In biblical language, it is one who opposes God or His people: when the Lord withdraws from Saul, he becomes His "enemy" (1 Samuel 28:16), not because he physically fights him, but because he has set himself against him and no longer supports him.
H6145.origine: The Hebrew word עָר (ar) primarily means one who looks askance, who "watches" against someone with hostility. It is a simple word in biblical Hebrew, unrelated to other roots. It designates the adversary, the one to be wary of.
H6145.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible according to the provided usages. In 1 Samuel 28:16, Samuel tells Saul that the Lord, by withdrawing from him, has become his enemy: this conveys the idea that a friend can become an adversary if God allows it. In Psalms 139:20, God's enemy is one who slanders and abuses the name of the Lord. The word always designates a personal or spiritual adversary, never a mere difference of opinion.
H6145.portee: Understanding who the biblical enemy is helps the reader grasp that hostility is not only physical: it can be spiritual. When God withdraws from someone, it is the greatest danger. And every lie against God and His promises reveals an enemy heart. The word invites the believer to remain faithful so as not to oppose the Lord.

sens: person who opposes someone, who is hostile to them
H6146.detail: 1. Adversary designates someone who opposes another person, who is contrary or hostile to them. It is an enemy in the active sense: one who seeks to harm or is in conflict. Daniel, reporting the dream of the king of Babylon, wishes that this dream concerns the king's enemies, his adversaries (Daniel 4:19) — that is, those who are opposed to him.
H6146.origine: The Aramaic word עָר (ar) is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word עַר (ar, H6145), which means enemy or adversary. Both forms share the same root and designate one who is against, who obstructs. The Aramaic ar is used in the Aramaic sections of the book of Daniel.
H6146.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 4:19, where Daniel responds to King Nebuchadnezzar. In this instance, adversary is contrasted with enemy (the same passage mentions both forms): both refer to those who oppose the king. The context is that of interpreting a troubling dream, and Daniel prays that his misfortune be turned toward the adversaries of the sovereign.
H6146.portee: This word shows us that in the Bible, the adversary is not an abstraction: it is a real person, an opposing will. For the Christian, this invites recognition that there are forces and people who oppose his interests, and to pray, like Daniel, for God to protect him from his adversaries and to turn them away.

sens: Firstborn son of Judah and Bath-Shua
Man judged wicked by the Lord
The one whose death the Lord caused
H6147G.detail:
1. Er is the first son of Judah, born from his union with the Canaanite Bath-Shua (Genesis 38:3). He has two younger brothers, Onan and Shelah, and becomes the father of a lineage that will not flourish according to God's plan.
2. The Bible describes him as "wicked in the eyes of the Lord" (Genesis 38:7). This moral condemnation is unequivocal: he committed evil in the sight of the Lord, which provokes his punishment.
3. The Lord caused him to die prematurely (Genesis 38:7), without living descendants. His death, also reported in Numbers 26:19 and 1 Chronicles 2:3, marks divine rejection and opens the way for the complex saga of Tamar and Onan.
H6147G.origine: The name Er means "watchman" or "one who watches," from the Hebrew verb עור (ûr). It is an auspicious name — one would expect a vigilant, responsible son — but the man will not live up to this destiny. The irony of the name highlights his judgment: the one who was to watch over the honor of his house proves unworthy.
H6147G.emploi: Er appears only in six passages (Genesis 38:3, 38:6, 38:7; Genesis 46:12; Numbers 26:19; 1 Chronicles 2:3), all concentrated around the story of Judah and Tamar or in genealogical lists. Each mention ties him to his family — as the son of Judah, husband of Tamar — and to his death. He embodies the man condemned for his wickedness, whose demise leaves a distressed widow and creates the paradoxical situation where Onan must ensure Er's descendants. His lack of direct offspring contrasts with the line of Perez, which prospers.
H6147G.portee: Er reminds us that social position and lineage do not protect against divine judgment: we do not know precisely his fault, but his wickedness was enough to cut him off. His fate invites moral vigilance, exactly what his name promises. The narrative also reveals hidden mercy: through Tamar and Perez, a faithful lineage emerges, including King David, showing that God redeems and restores what man has perverted.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, son of Shelah and grandson of Judah
H6147H.detail: Er is a descendant of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:21. He is the son of Shelah and the grandson of Judah, and he had a son named Lekah. He is also the brother of Laadah, Jokim, Joash, and Saraph. This genealogical passage situates Er among the families of Judah who distinguished themselves by their work with fine linen, a precious fabric.
H6147H.origine: The name Er means "the one who watches" or "vigilant," evoking the idea of being awake or attentive. It is a simple Hebrew name, borne by at least two individuals in the Old Testament: this Er of the tribe of Judah, and another Er who was the firstborn son of Judah (mentioned in Genesis 38). The genealogical context of 1 Chronicles 4:21 shows that Er was a man of Judah established in Canaan.
H6147H.emploi: Er appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:21, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Judah. This passage enumerates the ancestors and families who excelled in the work of fine linen, a highly valued textile. Er is presented as the genealogical link between his father Shelah and his son Lekah, thus inscribing his lineage in the history of the people of Judah.

sens: To act as a guarantor for someone, to take responsibility in case of default
To give a pledge or guarantee in exchange for an obligation
To mix, unite, or establish a link between two things or people
To commit, promise, accept a burden or responsibility
To have a bond of covenant or communion
H6148.detail:
1. To act as a guarantor for someone: this means taking on the responsibility that another person fulfills their promise or debt. Judah says to Jacob: "I will be responsible for him" (Genesis 43:9) — he puts his own life at stake to guarantee that his younger brother Benjamin will return safely. This is the most serious commitment: if Benjamin does not return, Judah accepts to be guilty in his place.
2. To give a pledge or guarantee: this means handing over something of value in exchange for a promise or credit. In Proverbs 20:16, the one who has guaranteed a stranger must leave his garment as a pledge; this is the concrete price of his recklessness.
3. To mix or unite: the word also describes the act of mingling with others, losing one's distinct identity. After the return from exile, Ezra denounces those who "have mingled the holy race with the peoples of these lands" (Ezra 9:2) — this is a covenant or communion that erases boundaries.
4. To commit or promise: this means accepting an obligation, binding oneself by a word. The word appears in contexts of agreement or convention between parties.
5. To have a bond of communion: in its most intimate sense, the word designates sharing, communion in a covenant or shared responsibility.
H6148.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "mixing" or "binding together." The family of the word includes forms that emphasize mutual exchange or sharing of a common responsibility. The basic image is that of two things or two people tying themselves to one another — either through a material bond (a pledge) or through a moral commitment (a guarantee). It is a very Hebrew word: it expresses the solidarity of the clan or family, where each one is responsible for the others.
H6148.emploi: The word appears 22 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Wisdom literature (Proverbs 6 times) and in the accounts of the return from exile (Ezra, Nehemiah). It is used primarily in a legal and commercial sense: to guarantee a debt, to give a pledge, to take personal responsibility (Proverbs 11:15, 20:16, 22:26). The meaning extends to the social domain: to mix one's strengths or interests with others (Psalms 106:35, Ezra 9:2, Proverbs 24:21). In the context of supplication or prayer, the word describes the act of committing to respond or appear before God (Psalms 119:122, Job 17:3). In the prophets, it takes on a political significance: Ezekiel 27 lists those who "guarantee" or bind themselves to Tyre through trade and alliance.
H6148.portee: This word invites the Christian to meditate on the responsibility we take when we commit ourselves to others. Judah in Genesis 43:9 illustrates total devotion: to be a guarantor is to put one's life in place of another's. It is also an image of what Jesus did: he became our guarantor, our advocate before God. On the other hand, the word warns against the dangers of a bad alliance: mingling with those who do not share our faith risks losing our identity and testimony. There is wisdom in choosing our commitments carefully.

sens: That which pleases the senses, which is sweet and enjoyable
That which satisfies the soul, which is suitable for someone
That which is acceptable, welcome, approved
That which attracts preference or desire
H6149.detail:
1. The concrete meaning of "sweet" or "pleasant": something that charms the senses or provides well-being. A sweet sleep is a restful and peaceful sleep (Proverbs 3:24). A fulfilled desire is pleasant to the soul because it fulfills and calms it (Proverbs 13:19).
2. What pleases God or someone: a person or an offering is pleasant when it gains approval. The burnt offerings of the Israelites are not pleasant to God because He rejects their insincere worship (Jeremiah 6:20).
3. What is suitable or satisfying in a relationship: a companion with whom one is "pleased," meaning one wants to remain united. It is also a sleep that has truly done good, which one will remember fondly (Jeremiah 31:26).
4. It is a word that describes the impression one feels when something or someone meets our expectations or desires, on a physical, emotional, or spiritual level.
H6149.origine: The Hebrew root עָרַב (a.rev) fundamentally evokes what is sweet, pleasant to the taste. It has given rise to other forms to designate sweetness or what is mixed (as sugar mixes). In Greek, this verb was often translated by terms meaning "to please" or "to be pleasant." It is a word that starts from concrete sensory experience — the taste of sugar — to expand to everything that provides pleasure or satisfaction.
H6149.emploi: This Hebrew verb appears 8 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms, Proverbs, and the prophets. It first describes what is physically pleasant: a sweet sleep (Proverbs 3:24), a pleasing word (Psalms 104:34). It then expands to the spiritual realm: God approving or rejecting worship (Jeremiah 6:20, Malachi 3:4). It also applies to human relationships: the one with whom one is "pleased" (Ezekiel 16:37). In each case, the word carries the idea that a thing or a person pleases or should please, that it gains approval or desire.
H6149.portee: This word invites the reader to understand that God does not accept worship out of habit or routine: the offering must be pleasant in His eyes, meaning sincere and loving. It also reminds us that the Christian life touches on small things — a restful sleep, a just word — and that there is a spiritual beauty in seeking what is truly good and pleasant, not out of selfishness, but out of a taste for the true, the good, and the beautiful.

sens: To reach the moment when the day declines and night comes
To get late in the day
To lack, to be missing (figurative sense)
H6150.detail:
1. The word describes the moment when the day declines and evening arrives: it is the transition from day to night. In Judges 19:9, a man is about to leave, but he is told, "the day is declining, it is getting late" — evening is approaching, it is time to stop. It is a natural observation of the rhythm of the day.
2. The word can also simply refer to the moment of evening, as in 1 Samuel 17:16 where the Philistine presents himself "morning and evening" — he appears twice a day, at dawn and at dusk. Here, "evening" names the part of the day.
3. Figuratively, the word can mean "to lack" or "to be missing," as in Isaiah 24:11 where "the wine is lacking" — the idea of disappearance, absence, brings this meaning close to the first: just as light fades in the evening, here what should be present flows away and disappears.
H6150.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of mixing or blurring. As evening approaches, light and darkness mix; hence the image of evening as a moment of transition. This same root also gives words related to Arabic or the trade of caravans at dusk.
H6150.emploi: This verb appears only three times in the Bible. It first describes the natural moment when the day ends and night comes (Judges 19:9). It can also simply refer to the evening period as a part of the day (1 Samuel 17:16). Once, it takes a figurative sense and means "to lack" or "to be missing" (Isaiah 24:11), where the disappearance of wine symbolizes a lack of joy. The word is thus both very concrete and capable of carrying a more abstract meaning.
H6150.portee: This word reminds the reader of the rhythm created by God of day and night, a fundamental alternation of human life. It also emphasizes how even concrete moments — the approach of evening — invite reflection and rest. Its figurative sense of "to lack" or "to disappear" invites meditation on what we truly lack and on the goods that pass away.

sens: To blend together, to bring into close contact
To unite by bonds, to form an alliance
To combine distinct elements without complete union
H6151.detail:
1. To mix means to blend two or more things together, placing them in contact with each other. In Nebuchadnezzar's dream, iron mixed with clay (Daniel 2:41) describes a mixture of two materials that have been fused, like when mixing two powders or two liquids.
2. The word can express an alliance or union between peoples or persons. In Daniel 2:43, the peoples "will mix through human alliances": it is the image of mixing applied to social and political bonds.
3. To mix emphasizes that two things are joined, but not necessarily in a stable or lasting way. Daniel 2:43 adds: "they will not be united one to another, just as iron does not adhere to clay" — the mixture is superficial, without true cohesion.
H6151.origine: The Hebrew verb עֲרַב (arav) comes from a root that evokes the idea of crossing, mixing, or pouring together. In Hebrew, the same family of words can designate a guarantor or a pledge (עָרוּב : aroub), the common idea being one of interpenetration or mutual involvement. The word refers to the concrete action of mixing substances.
H6151.emploi: The verb appears only twice in Daniel 2:41-43, both in the interpretation of the dream of the statue with feet of clay and iron. The apocalyptic nature of the context (a prophetic dream) and the repetition structure the passage: iron "mixed" with clay is first presented as an observable fact (verse 41), then reinterpreted as a symbol of human alliances that will lack solidity (verse 43). The term emphasizes the instability of future kingdoms — an apparent mixture but devoid of true unity.
H6151.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the nature of alliances and unions among men. The mixture of iron and clay, although visible, is declared non-durable: this reminds us that purely human bonds, without a transcendent foundation, lack true strength. For the Christian, it is an exhortation not to seek a false unity with what is spiritually incompatible, but to seek a solid alliance founded in God.

sens: Desert region of the Middle East, vast arid plateau
H6152A.detail: 1. Arabia is a large region of the Middle East characterized by its vast deserts and arid high plateaus. In the Bible, this term particularly refers to the territory located south and east of Palestine. Isaiah 21:13 mentions the thickets of Arabia, recalling the inhospitable nature of these lands where merchant caravans travel.
H6152A.origine: The Hebrew word עֲרַב (arav) comes from a root evoking aridity and desolation. The term literally designates the arid region par excellence, known as a land of steppes and deserts where nomadic peoples live and where major trade routes pass.
H6152A.emploi: The word appears in the Bible to describe this desert region. Isaiah 21:13 uses it in a prophetic oracle announcing judgments against Arabia, particularly mentioning the caravans of Dedan, merchants who traversed these arid lands. The context evokes the difficulty of traveling through this desert, where travelers must seek refuge in the thickets.
H6152A.portee: Arabia reminds the reader that even the most hostile and remote regions are under God's watch and subject to His prophetic word. This name also evokes the challenges of the spiritual journey and the importance of the trade routes that connected ancient peoples.

sens: desert region to the east and south of Canaan
nomadic people of the steppes and desert
H6152B.detail:
1. Arabia is the vast desert region that extends to the east and south of the territory of Israel. It is a land of arid steppes where the Bedouins, these nomadic shepherd peoples, live. The kings of Arabia are mentioned as important trade partners: Solomon receives gold and silver from them (2 Chronicles 9:14).
2. The word also refers to the peoples who inhabit these steppes, the nomadic Arabs of the desert. Jeremiah speaks of "all the kings of Arabia and all the kings of the Arabs who dwell in the desert" (Jeremiah 25:24), showing that these desert peoples are organized into kingdoms and tribes led by princes.
H6152B.origine: The Hebrew word literally means "steppe-dwellers," that is, the inhabitants of arid steppes. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of desert and nomadism. This name reflects the geographical and cultural reality: this people lives in arid and semi-desert lands, moving with their flocks according to pastures and water points.
H6152B.emploi: Arabia appears four times in the Old Testament, always as a commercial and political power on the fringes of the known world of Israel. In the time of Solomon, the kings of Arabia are part of the tributary or partner states that bring gold and silver to the kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 10:15 and 2 Chronicles 9:14). In the time of Jeremiah, God announces that His anger will also reach "all the kings of Arabia" (Jeremiah 25:24). Ezekiel describes Arabia as a trading partner of Tyre, trafficking in lambs, rams, and goats (Ezekiel 27:21), which shows the economic role of this people of nomadic shepherds.
H6152B.portee: Arabia reminds the reader that the people of God are not isolated: they live in a network of nations and peoples, some friends, others subject to God's judgment. These allusions to Arabia also show that the wealth and power of Solomon do not come solely from Israel, but from the honor that neighboring nations give him. It is a sign of the success of the reign blessed by God.

sens: the time of day when the sun sets, the transition from light to darkness
the night, the darkness that follows sunset
the west, the direction where the sun sets
H6153.detail:
1. Evening is the precise moment when light disappears and darkness begins: it is twilight or sunset. In Genesis 1:5, after the creation of light and darkness, Moses notes "there was evening, and there was morning" to mark the divisions of the day. This evening marks the end of one period and the entry into another.
2. The word also refers to the entire night, the darkness that reigns after sunset. In Leviticus 15:11 and Numbers 19:8, a person becomes "unclean until evening," which means that their impurity persists during the night and is removed with the new day. Job 7:4 speaks of a long night of insomnia, saying "when will the night end?".
3. Rarely, the word can refer to the west, the place from which evening comes, that is, the direction of sunset: this is the directional meaning of the word.
H6153.origine: The Hebrew word עֶרֶב comes from a root that evokes the idea of mixing or intertwining: evening is the moment when light and darkness mix. This same root can also evoke what is mixed or confused, hence "night" (darkness, confusion). It is a fundamental word in biblical Hebrew, used more than one hundred twenty-five times to structure time according to the creation narratives and ritual laws.
H6153.emploi: The word first appears in Genesis to structure the days of creation: "there was evening, and there was morning" (Genesis 1:5, 1:8, 1:13, etc.). In the Law, it marks the expiration of periods of purity or impurity: a person remains unclean "until evening" (Leviticus 15:11, Numbers 19:8). It also sets the hours for offerings to the Lord (Exodus 29:39, Numbers 28:4). Finally, it designates the moments when one travels or gathers: Genesis 24:11 speaks of Eliezer's arrival "at evening time." The word thus structures the real time of the Hebrew people and their religious life.
H6153.portee: Evening reminds us of the natural oscillation between the work of the day and the rest of the night. For the believer, it also evokes finitude: each evening closes a day that will not return. The laws of impurity related to evening teach that time is a factor of purification and renewal. The regular cycle of day and night reveals the wisdom and order of the Creator.

sens: desert region of the Middle East, to the south and east of the Holy Land
H6154A.detail: 1. Arabia is the vast desert region that extends to the south and east of Canaan. The Hebrew word evokes this territory and its inhabitants, the Arabs. In Jeremiah 25:24, the kings of Arabia are mentioned among the nations that God will judge by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar: it is a reminder that even distant peoples are not beyond the reach of divine judgment.
H6154A.origine: The Hebrew word עֵרֶב (erev) literally means "mixture" or "mixed people," as Arabia was populated by diverse and nomadic tribes. This sense of "mixture" reflects the cosmopolitan character of this territory. The word can also refer to the Arabs themselves, these desert peoples.
H6154A.emploi: The word appears twice in the Old Testament: in Jeremiah 25:24 and Ezekiel 30:5. In these two prophetic passages, Arabia is among the nations that will undergo God's judgment. Biblical texts often mention the Arabs as desert peoples, warriors and traders, distinct from established nations. Jeremiah speaks of "the kings of Arabia" and "the kings of the Arabs who dwell in the desert," showing that it is a politically fragmented region made up of tribal kingdoms.
H6154A.portee: Arabia reminds the reader that God governs not only Israel and the great powers (Egypt, Babylon), but also the distant and nomadic peoples of the desert. This affirms the universality of God's plan over history.

sens: the threads that run horizontally in a fabric, interwoven with the warp
the entire fabric when it bears a stain or a ritual disease
H6154B.detail:
1. The weft is the part of the woven fabric: these are the threads that pass from one side to the other of the loom, interwoven with the warp threads that run lengthwise. Together, the warp and weft form the compact fabric. It is this structure that the law of Moses examines precisely in Leviticus 13:48, where the priest inspects whether a leprous spot has spread "to the warp or to the weft."
2. By extension, the word also refers to the garment or leather object itself when it is affected by disease. In Leviticus 13:52, if the leprosy has penetrated the fabric, one must burn "the warp or the weft of wool or linen," that is, the entire contaminated garment, because the disease has rendered it irreparably unclean.
H6154B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to mix" or "to intertwine." The weft gets its name from the fact that it is interlaced with the warp: the two systems of threads cross and mix to form a tight fabric. This image of intertwining and mixing is found in other uses of the same root in Hebrew.
H6154B.emploi: The word appears 9 times in Leviticus, exclusively in chapters 13 and 58, which deal with the laws of purity concerning leprosy. It is a technical term of textiles: the priest must examine whether a leprous spot extends "to the warp or to the weft" to decide if the garment is clean or unclean (Leviticus 13:48-56). If the disease has truly penetrated the fabric, the entire object must be burned (Leviticus 13:52). This constant repetition of the pair "warp or weft" shows that the law scrutinizes the fabric in all its dimensions to detect ritual contamination.
H6154B.portee: This word reminds us of the importance that the law of Moses places on purity, even in the material details of daily life. The meticulous inspection of the weft of a garment shows that nothing escapes God's gaze and that holiness comes through order and clarity. For the Christian, this evokes the totality of purification: Christ does not only restore appearance but transforms everything He touches, deeply.

sens: Heterogeneous crowd of people from diverse origins mixed together
Foreign peoples or elements mixed with a main people
Fabric or material interwoven with different threads
H6154M.detail:
1. This word refers to a crowd made up of people coming from everywhere, without a unified origin. At the Exodus from Egypt, it was not only the Hebrews who left the country: "A mixed multitude went up with them" (Exodus 12:38), including Egyptians, slaves from other peoples, all mixed together in the same mass of fugitives.
2. By extension, the word can also refer to the foreign peoples or groups themselves when they are integrated or mixed with a main people. Thus in Nehemiah 13:3, "they separated from Israel all the foreigners": they expelled those who did not belong to the lineage of Israel, this mixture that blurred the identity of the people.
3. The word comes from the realm of weaving: it denotes the interlacing of threads of different colors or natures in a fabric, a perfect image of the mixing of peoples.
H6154M.origine: This Hebrew word is based on the image of interweaving (the warp and the weft of the fabric). In Hebrew, the root evokes mixing and intertwining. The same word can apply to both mixed peoples and the mixed threads of a fabric, as it carries the image of weaving to the composition of a crowd or community.
H6154M.emploi: This word appears infrequently in the Bible (4 occurrences), mainly in passages that describe periods of mixing or separation. In Exodus 12:38, it refers to the mixed crowd fleeing Egypt with the Hebrews. In Nehemiah 13:3, after the exile, it is this mixture that Ezra and Nehemiah want to remove to purify Israel and preserve its identity. In Jeremiah 50:37 and Jeremiah 25:20, it describes the foreigners and diverse peoples in the heart of Babylon. Each time, the context emphasizes the tension between the unity of God's people and the presence of foreign elements.
H6154M.portee: This word invites reflection on the identity of God's people. It has never been a closed purity: from the Exodus from Egypt, all sorts of foreigners walked with Israel. But it is an identity that has contours, based on the covenant with God and the Law, not solely on ethnic origin. For the Christian, this word reminds us that the Church gathers people from diverse backgrounds, united not by blood but by faith.

sens: Tree of wet regions, with flexible branches and narrow leaves
Place planted with willows, generally near a watercourse
H6155G.detail:
1. The willow is a tree that naturally grows in areas where water is abundant, particularly near rivers and streams. It is characterized by its very flexible branches and long, narrow leaves, giving it a graceful and undulating appearance. It is a tree frequently encountered in Israel and throughout the ancient Near East.
2. In the Bible, the word "willow" also refers to the groves or thickets of willows that line the waterways and streams. In Isaiah 15:7, the "brook of willows" (literally: the "valley of willows") is a specific geographical location, probably a watercourse in the region of Moab, characterized by the presence of these trees.
H6155G.origine: The Hebrew word עֲרָבָה (aravah) comes from a root meaning "to be moist" or "to soak." The willow embodies this association with moisture and water, as this tree only grows where there is a certain abundance of water. In French, the word "willow" shares with Hebrew this obvious connection: the tree and water go together. The word also appears in names of biblical places.
H6155G.emploi: The word appears only once in the provided biblical text: in Isaiah 15:7, where the prophet describes the Moabites fleeing their land and taking their riches beyond the "brook of willows." This brook is mentioned as a geographical boundary, a watercourse that must be crossed. The context suggests a real and identifiable location at the time, known to the prophet's listeners as a natural landmark of the Moabite region. The use of the willow emphasizes here the importance of water and the natural boundaries of the territory.
H6155G.portee: The willow reminds the reader that in the Bible, trees and elements of nature are never insignificant backdrops: they mark places, delineate territories, and testify to the concrete geography where God's acts are fulfilled. This small detail contributes to the authenticity of the prophetic message.

sens: Tree with flexible branches that grows by the water's edge
Symbol of mourning and sadness in biblical poetry
H6155H.detail:
1. The willow is a real tree, characterized by its dark wood and long, supple branches. It naturally grows near waterways, streams, and springs. In Israel, it is found in wet valleys. In Leviticus 23:40, the willow is one of the four plants that the Israelites must take during the Feast of Tabernacles: its flexible branches easily combine with those of other trees (palms, myrtles) to form a leafy display before the Lord.
2. In biblical poetry, the willow evokes proximity to water and becomes an image of pain and sorrow. In Psalms 137:2, the exiles from Babylon hang their harps on the willows: this poetic detail expresses their misfortune and their inability to sing. The willow symbolizes affliction, as its presence by the watercourse recalls the tears shed.
H6155H.origine: The Hebrew word עֲרָבָה (aravah) comes from a root meaning "to be soft, flexible." The willow, with its long and supple branches that sway in the wind and above the water, embodies this flexibility. The basic image is that of a tree whose wood is soft and whose branches easily bend — hence its name in French "willow," from the Latin "salix." In Hebrew, the word reinforces the idea of malleability and aquatic life: a water tree that bends.
H6155H.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always to denote the real tree and its symbolic uses. In Leviticus 23:40, it is one of the trees of the Feast of Tabernacles, chosen for its branches that can be tied together. In Job 40:17 and Isaiah 44:4, the willow figures in images of life and prosperity near flowing water — the former in the description of the Behemoth surrounded by the willows of the brook, the latter in the promise that the people will multiply "like willows by the streams." In Psalms 137:2, finally, the willows become the tree of exile and desolation, a symbol of captivity where harps, instruments of joy, are silenced.
H6155H.portee: The willow teaches the Christian reader that God places beauty and abundance where living water flows — an image of His provision and blessing. The willow of the Tabernacles also reminds us that joy before the Lord can arise even from what is soft, flexible, and humble: it does not take the strength of the cedar to praise God. Finally, in Psalms 137, the willow invites reflection on legitimate mourning and faithfulness to God even in the midst of affliction: one does not renounce their faith in Israel and in their God, even in a foreign land.

sens: Pleasant to the taste, flavorful
Pleasant to the ear or senses
H6156.detail:
1. Pleasant to the taste, flavorful: the word describes what pleases the palate. In Proverbs 20:17, the bread of deceit is "sweet" — it first seduces by its appeal, like something good, before revealing its true bitter nature.
2. Pleasant to the ear or senses: the word extends to what charms through its beauty or harmony. The voice of the beloved is "sweet" in the Song of Songs (2:14), meaning delicate, melodious, pleasant to listen to.
H6156.origine: The Hebrew word עָרֵב comes from a root that expresses the idea of what pleases and attracts. It is a simple adjective that first designates pleasant flavor, then everything that seduces the senses. The same root has given the name "érèb" (evening), probably because evening is a time of rest and relaxation, hence the association with "sweet" or "pleasant." The word can also refer to exchange or barter (a "sweet" arrangement, mutually pleasing).
H6156.emploi: The word appears twice in the Old Testament, always in the sense of what pleases. In Proverbs 20:17, it qualifies a deceptive pleasure: deceit attracts first by its seductive charm ("sweet"), but its consequences are bitter. In Song of Songs 2:14, it describes sensual beauty: the voice of the beloved is "sweet," pleasant, desirable. In both cases, the word evokes immediate appeal, a seduction by the senses — what pleases at first glance.
H6156.portee: This word invites the believer to discern between immediate attraction and deep truth. As Proverbs 20:17 says, what is "sweet" in the present moment may prove destructive. It is a call to vigilance: not to be seduced by appearances, but to seek wisdom that lasts beyond fleeting pleasure. The word also reminds us that God creates true beauty — that which is sweet without deception.

sens: Winged insect that swarms and bites or stings
Manifestation of divine judgment against Egypt
Creature used by God to compel Pharaoh to free Israel
H6157.detail:
1. The word designates a fly or gnat that bites, probably a type of horsefly or biting fly: it is an annoying and dangerous insect that attacks the skin. The imagery of the Hebrew word emphasizes the chaotic aspect — these insects arrive in dense and uncontrollable swarms, like a writhing mixture from which one cannot escape (Exodus 8:17: "the houses of the Egyptians will be filled with flies, and the ground will be covered with them").
2. In the account of the plagues of Egypt, these flies are not merely a natural calamity: they embody the power of God who strikes and controls. They devour and destroy (Psalms 78:45: "He sent against them venomous flies that devoured them"), bringing devastation and helplessness.
3. It is an instrument of constraint: Pharaoh, unable to free himself from this plague, agrees to negotiate and is compelled to recognize the hand of the God of Israel. In Exodus 8:18, God shows that He controls this plague by preserving the land of Goshen where the people of Israel live — the flies thus become a sign of the distinction between those whom God protects and those whom He judges.
H6157.origine: The Hebrew word עָרֹב comes from a root that evokes mixture, confusion, and buzzing agitation. It is a concrete noun that literally paints a scene of chaos: countless and unpredictable flying insects intertwining in an incessant movement. The root emphasizes less the isolated insect than the phenomenon of swarming and invasion.
H6157.emploi: This word appears 7 times in the Bible, mainly in Exodus 8 (the fourth plague of Egypt: Exodus 8:17, 8:18, 8:20, 8:25, 8:27) and in the Psalms (Psalms 78:45 and 105:31, which recap the wonders of God and the plagues). In Exodus, the flies invade the houses of Pharaoh and his servants, devastate the land, and disappear at Moses' prayer — a precise manifestation of God's control over creation. Psalm 78 presents them as creatures that devour the Egyptians, highlighting the destructive and deadly aspect of divine judgment. Each occurrence shows a fly, or rather a swarm, as an agent of judgment and a test of power: that of Pharaoh (helpless) against that of the Lord (sovereign).
H6157.portee: For the Christian reader, these flies remind us that God is not distant or indifferent to oppression and injustice. He acts concretely, even through the smallest creatures, to free His own and to convince the powerful of the earth of His sovereignty. The distinction between the land of Goshen and the rest of Egypt also teaches that divine protection is real: it separates the children of God from those who reject Him, not out of caprice, but through just judgment.

sens: Black bird with shiny plumage, scavenger of carrion and seeds
Impure animal according to Mosaic Law
Creature lacking its own resources, dependent on God for its food
H6158.detail:
1. The raven is a medium-sized, recognizable black bird that frequents open spaces. Noah releases one from the ark to see if the waters have receded (Genesis 8:7), and the animal flies here and there, guided by its searching instinct.
2. In Moses' dietary code, the raven is counted among the unclean animals and forbidden for consumption (Leviticus 11:15 and Deuteronomy 14:14), reflecting the distinctive laws of the faith of Israel.
3. The raven becomes the image of one who neither sows nor reaps: God feeds it, as does the famished Elijah who receives bread and meat brought by ravens at the brook Cherith (1 Kings 17:4-6). This image underscores God's invisible providence.
H6158.origine: The Hebrew word עֹרֵב (orev) is a bird name probably related to the root meaning "to be yellow" or "to be pale," although the raven is black: perhaps a reference to the grayish hue of the soil where it lives, or to the beak and legs that are less dark. The word is ancient and found in the natural vocabulary of Genesis and the Levitical codes.
H6158.emploi: The raven appears ten times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in contexts of legal purity (Leviticus, Deuteronomy) and divine providence (1 Kings 17 with Elijah, Job 39, and Psalms 147 regarding the food provided by God). In Noah's case, it symbolizes the animal sent for reconnaissance. In Elijah's case, it becomes God's wonderful instrument to sustain the prophet in the wilderness. In the Psalms and Job, the raven illustrates the dependence of every creature on the Creator who provides for its needs without expectation of profit.
H6158.portee: The raven teaches the believer a humble lesson: like this bird that possesses nothing and does not work in the human sense, the disciple of Christ is called to trust God for his daily needs. The story of Elijah being fed by ravens concretely demonstrates that God never forsakes His faithful servant, regardless of the circumstances. This biblical detail invites one to detach the soul from material anxiety and to rely on God's goodness.

sens: Midianite military leader defeated by Gideon
Rock or battle site east of the Jordan where Oreb was killed
H6159.detail:
1. Oreb is one of the two leaders of the Midianite army that attacked Israel during the time of Gideon. He is captured and killed by the Ephraimites at the rock bearing his name (Judges 7:25). His name literally means "raven," but it primarily refers to this military commander, whose defeat remains memorable in the history of Israel.
2. The rock of Oreb is the site where this leader meets his death during the pursuit of the Midianites. This place becomes a geographical landmark — east of the Jordan — and a symbol of divine victory. Centuries later, the prophet Isaiah still alludes to it as an example of the Lord's power against His enemies (Isaiah 10:26).
H6159.origine: The name Oreb means "raven" in Hebrew, likely evoking a bird of prey or an omen animal. Although its literal meaning is animal-related, the word never refers to a raven in our texts: it remains the proper name of this Midianite leader and the rock of his downfall.
H6159.emploi: Oreb appears four times in the Bible. Judges 7:25 presents him as one of the two Midianite military leaders, captured and executed by the Ephraimites at the rock that now bears his name. Judges 8:3 mentions him again alongside Zeeb, to show that God delivered these enemies of Israel. Psalm 83:12 calls upon God to deal with Israel's enemies "like Oreb and Zeeb," as this victory remains an example of divine judgment. Finally, Isaiah 10:26 references it prophetically, stating that the Lord will strike His enemies "as He struck Midian at the rock of Oreb," proving that this event remains emblematic of divine deliverance.
H6159.portee: The victory over Oreb and his warriors shows how God delivers His enemies into the hands of His people, even when they seem outnumbered. For the believer, Oreb embodies the defeated enemy and serves as a reminder that God never fails in His promise of protection.

sens: the great desert valley that extends from the south of the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea and beyond
H6160G.detail: The Arabah is the major geographical depression of the ancient Near East: an arid and barren valley that begins below the Sea of Galilee, descends along the Jordan, encompasses the Dead Sea, and extends to the Gulf of Aqaba. It is a region of desert plains and steppes, often scorching and inhospitable. In biblical narratives, the Arabah marks the borders of Israel's territory and serves as a geographical landmark: Moses speaks there before entering Canaan (Deuteronomy 1:1), armies maneuver there (Joshua 12:1), and fugitives seek refuge there (1 Samuel 23:24).
H6160G.origine: The Aramaic-Hebrew word אֲרָבָה (aravah) literally means "desert plain" or "steppe." It evokes aridity and the absence of abundant plant life. The name designates a real geographical region, well known to the ancient Israelites as a passage and refuge area, characterized by its extreme dryness.
H6160G.emploi: The Arabah appears 21 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the historical and prophetic books. It is first mentioned in Moses' speech (Deuteronomy 1:1, 1:7) as a landmark of the Israelites' journey to Canaan. The conquest narratives regularly place it as a boundary or area of military operations (Joshua 8:14, 11:2, 11:16, 12:1-3, 12:8). David and his men cross it or hide there while fleeing Saul (1 Samuel 23:24, 2 Samuel 2:29, 2 Samuel 4:7). Later, the prophets refer to it during times of national catastrophe, notably the fall of Jerusalem (2 Kings 25:4, Jeremiah 39:4, 52:7). Ezekiel situates eschatological visions there (47:8), and Zechariah mentions it in his final prophetic picture (14:10).
H6160G.portee: The Arabah reminds Christians that God leads His people through difficult and often inhospitable regions. It is a terrain of rigor, trial, and dependence on divine guidance. It also symbolizes the concrete and earthly nature of God's plan: the covenant was embodied in real geography, and salvation passes through places of transition and struggle.

sens: the great arid valley that extends from the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea and beyond
desert region and steppe
H6160H.detail:
1. The Arabah is the great depression that forms the natural boundary between Transjordan (to the east) and the territory of Israel (to the west). This valley, cut by the Jordan and the Dead Sea, is an arid and inhospitable area. The prophet Amos mentions it to signify the extent of God's judgment: the borders of Israel will be reduced to the shores of this wild region (Amos 6:14).
2. The word more broadly designates a desert and barren land, a steppe or desert: it is a space devoid of life, water, and resources — the very image of ruin and abandonment that God inflicts on an unfaithful people.
H6160H.origine: The Hebrew word עֲרָבָה (arabah) comes from a root that evokes desiccation and nakedness. It geographically designates the great rift valley that runs through the Levant from north to south. This geographical proper name has also been used as a common noun for any desert or desolate region. The underlying image is that of a bare terrain, without shelter or resources.
H6160H.emploi: The Arabah is mentioned once in the provided usages, in Amos 6:14, where the prophet announces that the Northern Kingdom (Israel) will be reduced to the borders of the Arabah — that is, dispossessed of its conquered territories, brought back to its narrowest limits, at the edge of the desert. It is an image of punishment: losing the Arabah means losing almost everything. This arid area symbolizes for Amos a horizon of desolation and reduction.
H6160H.portee: For the biblical reader, the Arabah reminds us that geography itself speaks of God's judgment. It is in this desert that the eastern shore of the Dead Sea extends, a natural boundary laden with meaning: a line between salvation and ruin, between inheritance and exile. Understanding the Arabah helps grasp the urgency and gravity of the prophetic threat.

sens: desert region east of the Jordan, opposite Jericho
territory of refuge for the Israelites at the end of the Exodus
H6160I.detail: The Plain of Moab is the vast flat and arid region located east of the Jordan, opposite Jericho. It is here that the Israelites set up camp at the end of their desert crossing, before crossing the Jordan to enter the Promised Land (Numbers 33:48-49). Moses dies there and is buried (Deuteronomy 34:1, 34:8). This territory later becomes the inheritance of the tribe of Reuben and that of Gad (Numbers 32).
H6160I.origine: The Hebrew word *araváh* literally means "desert" or "desert plain" — it describes the flat and arid regions of the Levant. Here, it is specified by the addition of "of Moab" to designate this particular plain. The word appears elsewhere in the Bible for other desert regions (like the plain of the Jordan), but this mention in Numbers and Deuteronomy becomes a major geographical landmark.
H6160I.emploi: The term appears about a dozen times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in the book of Numbers and Deuteronomy. It designates the camp where Israel stays after crossing the desert of the Exodus, before the conquest of Canaan. It is here that wars against Midian are conducted (Numbers 31), that the lands of Transjordan are distributed to the tribes (Numbers 32-36), and where Moses dies and is mourned (Deuteronomy 34). This place symbolizes the final stage of the journey toward the fulfillment of the promise.
H6160I.portee: This place reminds the reader that the fulfillment of God's promises is never immediate. The Israelites wait at the Plain of Moab before crossing the Jordan, just as believers often must wait and persevere before seeing God's promises fulfilled. It is also the place where Moses, after leading the people for forty years, cannot himself enter the Promised Land — a lesson on obedience and its limits.

sens: desert region of Palestine, on the edge of the Jordan Valley
H6160J.detail: 1. Araba is an arid and steppe region of the Near East, located near the Jordan Valley. It refers to a desert plain area, which is poorly fertile and hostile. In Joshua 18:18, the boundary of the tribe of Benjamin runs along this region: the limit "passed on the northern side opposite Araba, descended to Araba," which shows that Araba is a clearly identifiable geographical area, recognizable on the ground as a reference point for delineating tribal lands.
H6160J.origine: The Hebrew word עֲרָבָה (araba) literally means "barren place" or "desert." It comes from a root that evokes dryness and desolation. This term specifically designates the steppes and arid lands of the Near East, particularly the depression that runs along the course of the Jordan, from the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea and beyond. It is a well-known and real geography to the Israelites.
H6160J.emploi: The word appears only once in this context of territorial delimitation in Joshua 18:18. Araba is mentioned as a geographical marker used to define the boundaries of the tribe of Benjamin. It is a desert region but precisely identified in Palestinian geography, notable enough to be used as an official reference point during the land distribution after the conquest.
H6160J.portee: For the Christian reader, Araba reminds us that the Promised Land includes difficult, hostile regions, where life requires trust in God rather than in natural resources. It is an element of the real geography where the history of salvation unfolded.

sens: desert and depressed region south of the Dead Sea
H6160K.detail: 1. The Arabah is a vast geographical depression that extends south of the Dead Sea, towards the Gulf of Aqaba. It is an arid and low region, characterized by a desert climate. The name also refers, by extension, to the Dead Sea itself, which was also called the "Salt Sea." In Joshua 3:16, the Arabah appears as a well-identified region during the crossing of the Jordan: the waters "descended" as they moved from higher ground to the depression of the Arabah. In 2 Kings 14:25, it is mentioned as a geographical boundary of the restored kingdom of Israel.
H6160K.origine: The Hebrew word עֲרָבָה (aravah) literally designates a "barren" or "empty" region, evoking the aridity of the desert. It likely comes from a root expressing desolation. It is a specific geographical term that becomes a proper name to designate this great valley of the Levant, one of the lowest regions in the world.
H6160K.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible provided here. In Joshua 3:16, it refers to the region of the Dead Sea during Israel's miraculous crossing of the Jordan. In 2 Kings 14:25, it marks a boundary of the territory restored by Jeroboam II. This proper geographical name remains stable in its uses: it always refers to this characteristic natural depression of the Levant.

sens: the great desert depression that extends from the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea and beyond
