a desert or arid steppe
H6160L.detail: 1. The Arabah is primarily a well-known geographical region: the great depressed valley that runs north to south in the Holy Land, from the shores of the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea and further towards the Red Sea. It is an extremely arid and inhospitable terrain. Joshua 4:13 and 2 Samuel 15:28 show people crossing this region. 2. By extension, the word designates any desert or steppe without water and vegetation, a place of desolation. Isaiah 35:1 speaks of the Arabah rejoicing and blooming, a poetic image of miraculous transformation; Jeremiah 17:6 compares the unfaithful man to a solitary plant in the Arabah, unable to survive. These passages show the word used to evoke dryness and isolation.
H6160L.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that likely evokes dryness and desolation. The Arabah is primarily the name of a famous geographical region, the great depression of the African Rift in the Holy Land. It is not just a common word for "desert," but the name of a specific place that has come to symbolize all arid and inhospitable terrain in biblical language.
H6160L.emploi: The word appears about twenty times in the Old Testament, especially in the prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah) and in historical narratives (2 Samuel, 2 Kings, Joshua). It primarily designates the concrete geographical location where the Bible situates events: King David and the Prophet Jeremiah flee or hide there (2 Samuel 15:28; Jeremiah 39:5). But it also carries a symbolic and theological weight: the Arabah becomes the image of misery, sin, or absence of grace (Jeremiah 2:6, where God reminds that He guided the people "through the desert"), and also the place where God acts in salvation and transformation (Isaiah 35:1-6, where the desert blooms again as a sign of forgiveness). The word thus constantly balances between precise geographical meaning and spiritual significance.
H6160L.portee: For the reader, the Arabah teaches that God governs even the most remote and barren places: He guides His people there, pursues fugitives there, and even transforms dryness into fruitfulness. It is a call to see God's hand everywhere, even in apparent silence, and a promise that the Lord can bring life to what seems dead. The mention of the Arabah also recalls the trials of the desert that God's people had to endure to be shaped and purified.

sens: To act as a guarantor for someone with a creditor or authority
To take on a commitment on behalf of another, at the risk of one's own assets
H6161.detail:
1. To act as a guarantor for someone with a creditor or authority: this means promising to pay or respond if the other cannot do so. In Proverbs 17:18, the man without sense puts himself in this dangerous position by guaranteeing for his neighbor — he agrees to pay another's debt if that person does not settle it.
2. To take on a commitment on behalf of another, at the risk of one's own assets: guaranteeing is a voluntary but risky act, as one exposes their wealth. It is a gesture of trust towards someone, but it can lead to ruin if the other does not keep their promises.
H6161.origine: The Hebrew word arubba comes from the root arab which suggests an exchange, an arrangement between two people. It designates the pledge or the asset offered as a guarantee, then the act of acting as a guarantor itself. It is a legal term from the ancient commercial world, where personal guarantees sealed agreements between creditor and borrower.
H6161.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times to describe an act of personal guaranteeing. In 1 Samuel 17:18, Jesse asks David to bring to his brothers a guarantee of grain and bread — here the meaning is that of a present or pledge. In Proverbs 17:18, it refers to guaranteeing in the full sense: taking responsibility for another's debt, which the wise warns against as folly. The word emphasizes the idea of engaged responsibility and personal exposure each time.
H6161.portee: Guaranteeing speaks to those who must learn prudence: the Proverb warns that lightly binding oneself for another, without discernment, is to run into disaster. It is an invitation to wisdom in our commitments, and a reminder that our promises have a real cost. For the Christian, this also resonates with the call to justice and mutual responsibility in the community.

sens: object given as security for a debt or promise
material proof of a commitment
H6162.detail:
1. An object left with someone as a guarantee that a promise will be kept or a debt repaid. It serves as a kind of collateral: as long as the promise is not fulfilled, the creditor retains the object. In Genesis 38:18, Judah promises Tamar to send a goat, and he leaves his seal, cord, and staff as a pledge—very precious personal items—until he fulfills his promise.
2. More broadly, it serves as proof and a bond of commitment: the object given establishes that there is a real obligation between two parties. The pledge binds both parties until satisfaction is achieved.
H6162.origine: The Hebrew word ʿaravôn comes from a root that evokes the idea of intertwining or mutual engagement: giving a pledge creates a tangible link between two wills. This word has passed into Greek as ἀρραβών (arrabôn), where it took on the specific meaning of earnest or security deposit in contracts.
H6162.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, all in the story of Judah and Tamar (Genesis 38). Judah promises to send a goat to the woman who approached him on the road; not having it with him, he leaves personal items as a pledge—his seal, cord, and staff. These three instances describe the same type of transaction: a personal guarantee given until the promise is fulfilled. The context is one of a commercial or relational obligation that requires material assurance.
H6162.portee: This word speaks of seriousness and founded trust. When one gives a pledge, one puts something of oneself into the hands of another, which shows the reality of one’s commitment. For the believer, this reminds us of the importance of keeping one’s word and sealing commitments with visible, concrete actions—a lesson on honesty and respect for one’s promises.

sens: inhabitant of the deserts and steppes of the Arabian Peninsula
desert nomad
people of the ancient Near East
H6163A.detail: 1. The term primarily refers to the inhabitants of the arid and desert regions of Arabia, that is, the peoples who live between the desert and the cultivated lands of the Fertile Crescent. In Isaiah 13:20, the Arab is mentioned alongside the shepherds, highlighting that these are people accustomed to living in wild and sparsely populated spaces. 2. The word more broadly evokes the desert nomad: someone who does not settle in a city, who pitches their tent here and there to follow pastures and water. Jeremiah 3:2 uses it to describe someone who stands "in the desert," suggesting a mobile life without a stable dwelling. 3. At the geopolitical level, it is also a term that designates the Arab people as a distinct group from the Israelites and other neighboring nations of the Levant.
H6163A.origine: The word comes from the root עֲרָב (arab), which evokes the region of Arabia and its inhabitants. The French word "Arabe" is derived directly from it via Greek and Latin. The central notion is that of arid desert and the nomadic life that adapts to it; this is why the Bible often associates the Arab with the tent, herds, and boundless spaces.
H6163A.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Isaiah 13:20, it describes the desolation of a region—ruined Babylon—where even the nomadic Arab, accustomed to the most inhospitable lands, will no longer pitch his tent: it is an image of total abandonment. In Jeremiah 3:2, the prophet uses it as a comparison to illustrate Israel's unfaithfulness: like an Arab who stands in the desert, Israel has played the harlot on the paths. In both cases, the Arab embodies the desert nomad, a well-known figure to the Israelites.
H6163A.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible, composed in the ancient Near East, coexists with other peoples and cultures. It helps us visualize the landscapes and lifestyles of the biblical context: the cities of the Fertile Crescent are alongside the desert of Arabia and its mobile inhabitants. Recognizing the Arab in these verses is to enter into the geographical and human universe of God's people.

sens: Inhabitant of Arabia
Nomadic or semi-nomadic people of the Arabian desert
Ethnic group neighboring the territory of Israel
H6163B.detail:
1. The word designates an inhabitant or a member of a tribe from Arabia, a desert region to the south and east of Israel. In 2 Chronicles 17:11, the Arabs bring livestock as tribute to Jehoshaphat, showing that they were known for herding.
2. The Arabs in the biblical text are often nomadic or semi-nomadic peoples, warriors organized into tribal groups. In 2 Chronicles 21:16 and 22:1, they appear as destroyers, attacking alongside other peoples, thus demonstrating their military strength and ability to unite against Israel.
3. The Bible presents them as bordering and rival peoples, sometimes tributary, sometimes aggressive. In Nehemiah 2:19 and 4:7, Geshem the Arab and the Arabs oppose the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem, illustrating the tensions between the desert inhabitants and those of Judah.
H6163B.origine: The Hebrew word עַרְבִי (arvi) comes from the root עֲרָב (arab), which designates Arabia. This root evokes the Arabian desert, an arid and hostile region, the cradle of peoples with traditions and lifestyles distinct from those of Israel. The proper name "Arabia" appears in the Old Testament for this distant and mysterious region in the eyes of the Hebrews.
H6163B.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, only in the later historical books (2 Chronicles and Nehemiah). In 2 Chronicles, the Arabs are primarily depicted as tributaries or enemies: Jehoshaphat receives their tributes (17:11), but Joram and Ahaziah suffer their attacks (21:16; 22:1); Uzziah defeats some near Gur-Baal (26:7). In Nehemiah, written after the exile, Geshem the Arab and other Arabs become political adversaries of the temple reconstruction project (2:19; 4:7; 6:1). The context varies: tribute, war, political opposition, but the people remain distinct and significant in the history of Israel.
H6163B.portee: This word reminds us that God's people have interacted with other peoples, some hostile, others simply different. The Arabs embody the diversity of peoples with whom Israel had to negotiate or fight. For the Christian, this also illustrates the real biblical geography: Israel was not isolated, but at the crossroads of civilizations, enriching our understanding of the context of the events described in the Bible.

sens: inhabitant of Beth-Araba, a locality in Israel
H6164.detail: The word designates a man from Beth-Araba (which literally means "house of the desert"), a small town located in the arid lands east of the Jordan. In 2 Samuel 23:31, Azmaveth is presented as a warrior "of Araba," counting among the mighty men of King David. The same title appears in 1 Chronicles 11:32 to designate Abiel, also one of David's renowned fighters.
H6164.origine: The Hebrew word עַרְבָתִי (arvatí) derives from the name of the locality Beth-Araba (בֵּית הָעֲרָבָה), whose root עַרְבָה (arávah) means "desert" or "desert plain." The suffix -י (-í) forms an ethnic or geographical adjective, indicating origin or belonging to a place: it is a place-based patronymic, as found throughout the Bible to identify warriors by their hometown.
H6164.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, in two parallel places: 2 Samuel 23:31 and 1 Chronicles 11:32. It appears both times in the list of David's thirty heroes, the prominent warriors who followed and served him faithfully. These two occurrences designate different men (Azmaveth, then Abiel), but the title "of Araba" serves the same function: to clearly identify the warrior by his place of origin, a common practice in biblical lists of fighters.

sens: To experience an intense and painful desire for something, often expressing it through sighs
To cry out, to groan under the effect of strong emotion or deprivation
To languish, to wait with a deep aspiration
H6165.detail:
1. The word paints the image of a creature desiring something with all its intensity and expressing it through gestures or sounds. In Psalms 42:2, the deer that "longs for" water evokes both physical desire (thirst) and spiritual desire: my soul "longs for" God with the same strength. It is a desire that engages the whole being.
2. The word can also express a cry or a groan, particularly when deprivation or suffering is great. In Joel 1:20, the beasts of the field "cry out" to God because the streams are dry and fire has devoured the plains: they express their distress through cries in the face of drought.
3. The desire expressed here is not fleeting: it is a deep, constant aspiration, rooted in a vital dependence or lack.
H6165.origine: The word comes from a root that expresses the idea of stretching towards something, of extending in desire. In Hebrew, this verb evokes movement and emotion together: one does not long without the whole body being engaged. The initial image is that of the creature stretching, reaching out in desire.
H6165.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Psalms 42:2, the psalmist uses it to express the intense desire for God: it is a sigh of the heart, a spiritual thirst. In Joel 1:20, the beasts cry out because of the drought: the same verb expresses here the cry of distress of creatures deprived of water. In both cases, it is a desire or distress that is expressed with intensity and urgency.
H6165.portee: This word teaches us that the desire for God is not a vague or weak aspiration: it is a deep, vital thirst that engages our whole being, like a thirsty deer longs for water. It invites us to examine the strength and authenticity of our own desire for God, and to recognize in our own sighs and groans a legitimate prayer before the Lord.

sens: Canaanite royal city in southern Canaan
Region of the desert of Judah north of the Negev
H6166A.detail: 1. Arad is a royal city ruled by a Canaanite king, located in the southern part of the land of Canaan, near the desert of Judah. When Israel approaches from the desert, the king of Arad learns of their arrival and fights against the people, even capturing prisoners (Numbers 21:1). It is an enemy that the Israelites encounter during their conquest of the land. 2. The name also designates the surrounding region where this city was located, as Arad marks a geographical boundary: it is situated to the south of the desert of Judah, and it is towards this region that they travel (Judges 1:16).
H6166A.origine: The name literally means "a wild donkey" according to the Semitic root, an image of freedom and swift running. What was once a powerful royal city bears an animal name, probably due to the local significance of these creatures or the pride of the city. Archaeologically, Arad corresponds to a well-documented fortress city in southern Canaan.
H6166A.emploi: Arad appears four times in the Bible, always in the accounts of the conquest and settlement of Israel in Canaan. It first appears in Numbers 21:1, where its king opposes Israel coming out of the desert and fights against them. It reappears in Numbers 33:40 during the parallel account of the journey's stages, then in Joshua 12:14 among the list of kings defeated by Joshua. Finally, in Judges 1:16, Arad serves as a geographical landmark to locate where certain groups settled. The city holds military and strategic importance in the context of Israel's settlement.

sens: man of the tribe of Benjamin
H6166B.detail: Arad is a Benjamite character from the Old Testament, son of Beriah. He appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:15, in a genealogy of the descendants of Benjamin. His name literally means "a wild donkey" (the wild donkey is a species of wild ass). The Bible does not report any particular events from his life; he is simply listed among his brothers: Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth, Zebadiah, Eder, Michael, Ishpa, and Joha.
H6166B.origine: The name Arad comes from a Hebrew root designating the wild donkey, this robust and fierce animal of the desert. It was a name given to boys, perhaps evoking qualities like strength or wildness. It has no particular etymological link with other words in the same family.
H6166B.emploi: Arad is mentioned only once in the entire Bible: in 1 Chronicles 8:15. He appears in a genealogical list of the sons of Beriah, who himself was a member of the tribe of Benjamin. This genealogy lists the heads of families and valiant men who lived in Jerusalem. Arad is cited only for his belonging to this lineage, with no description of any action or personal characteristic concerning him.

sens: Wild animal of the equine species, living freely in arid regions
Figuratively, a state of degradation and bestiality in human beings
H6167.detail:
1. The wild donkey is an animal that lives freely in deserts and barren lands, unlike domestic donkeys that humans raise and control. It is an untamed, robust, and rustic beast. In Daniel 5:21, King Nebuchadnezzar, punished by God, "dwells with the wild donkeys" and eats grass like cattle: the image of the wild becomes a comparison of absolute humiliation.
2. The expression also describes the degradation of a man to an animal state, the loss of his reason and human dignity. When a king shares the fate of wild donkeys, he has lost not only his throne but his very humanity. It is the culmination of punishment: not merely a deposition, but a transformation into a creature without understanding.
H6167.origine: This Aramaic word (the language spoken by the Jews after the Babylonian exile) is the similar form of the Hebrew word עָרוֹד (h6171), which also designates the wild donkey. Both derive from a root denoting the idea of freedom and wandering. The word evokes the animal that runs freely in desert spaces, far from any human control, which makes it all the more symbolic when applied to a man: one moves from a rational creature to a wandering beast.
H6167.emploi: This word appears only once in the Aramaic of the New Testament (Daniel 5:21), in the passage reporting God's judgment on Nebuchadnezzar. The king, having become proud and forgetful of divine sovereignty, is struck with madness that brings him back to an animal state: for seven years, he lives like wild beasts, eats the grass of the fields, and his body is wet with the night dew. This unique occurrence carries a very strong theological weight: the wild donkey embodies here not just a simple creature, but the symbol of the humiliation that one deserves who rebels against God.
H6167.portee: This image of the king reduced to the state of a wild donkey reminds us of an essential truth: reason, dignity, and power do not belong to man by right, but come solely from God. He who becomes proud and rejects this dependence risks losing what defines him as a man. For the believer, it is a call to humility and recognition of divine sovereignty: our humanity itself depends on our submission to God.

sens: Remove clothing, make bare
Completely empty a container or place
Destroy, raze to the foundations
Reveal, expose what was hidden
Spread out, deploy widely
H6168.detail:
1. Remove clothing or make bare: the verb describes the action of undressing someone or leaving them unprotected. This is how Isaiah speaks of Kir who "makes bare" the shield by drawing it from its sheath (Isaiah 22:6), and the daughter of Edom will be "made bare" as a sign of humiliation and judgment (Lamentations 4:21).
2. Completely empty: when Rebekah empties her pitcher at the watering place (Genesis 24:20), she removes all the contents to pour it out. This is the same action the Lord takes in pouring humiliation upon Jerusalem (Isaiah 3:17).
3. Raze, demolish: to completely destroy a city or fortification, leaving it in ruins without any defense, as when walls are razed.
4. Reveal, uncover: to expose what was secret or hidden. The law speaks of "uncovering nakedness" to refer to forbidden sexual relations (Leviticus 20:19), that is, revealing intimacy.
5. Spread out, deploy: the wicked "spread out" like a green tree that occupies all the space (Psalms 37:35), an image of power and domination.
H6168.origine: The Hebrew verb ararah comes from a root that evokes the idea of stripping, leaving without covering or protection. It belongs to a family of words that express exposure and vulnerability. The initial image is physical: removing what covers or protects. It naturally extends to the idea of revealing, razing, emptying.
H6168.emploi: This verb appears 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in poetic and prophetic texts. It primarily denotes concrete actions: emptying a container (Genesis 24:20), razing fortifications (2 Chronicles 24:11), making shields bare in battle (Isaiah 22:6). However, it quickly takes on a metaphorical and theological meaning: exposing nakedness or shame (Leviticus 20:19), expressing divine judgment by stripping a city of its glory (Isaiah 3:17), or even describing abandonment and vulnerability (Psalms 141:8). In the Psalms, the word gains a spiritual significance: the one who pleads with God must not be "abandoned," meaning stripped of divine protection.
H6168.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God sees everything and cannot be deceived: nothing remains hidden before Him. It also awakens awareness of human fragility: we are naked and vulnerable without His protection. Finally, it warns of the reality of divine judgment: those who oppose God will be exposed and humiliated, while those who trust in Him will not be abandoned.

sens: State of being naked, uncovered, without clothing
Bare place or surface, deprived of what covered it
Absence of protection or resource
H6169.detail: 1. Nakedness refers to the state of being devoid of clothing or covering. In Isaiah 19:7, this term describes the bare and barren land along the Nile: the river, usually fertile and covered with lush vegetation, becomes completely stripped of plants. It is an image of total desolation, where everything that had been sown withers and disappears. 2. By extension, the word can refer to any place or surface that is in a state of abandonment or deprivation. It is the absence of what should cover or protect — here, the absence of harvest and plant life. 3. In a more figurative sense, nakedness can evoke vulnerability and the absence of protection against threats.
H6169.origine: The Hebrew word עָרָה (arah) comes from a root that evokes the idea of being uncovered or laid bare. It shares its root with other words in the Hebrew family denoting nakedness, exposure, or destitution. This term paints a concrete image: what was covered is now exposed, devoid of its usual covering.
H6169.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 19:7. In this passage, the prophet Isaiah announces God's judgment on Egypt: the Nile, a usual source of fertility and life, will be reduced to a state of total nakedness and sterility. The plants that should cover the riverbanks wither and disappear into dust. The image is that of a land completely stripped of its resources, becoming a dead land. This apocalyptic context gives the word all its force: nakedness is not just a state, but a sign of divine judgment.
H6169.portee: This image of nakedness and desolation reminds the reader that God has the power to withdraw His blessings and transform abundance into sterility. It invites reflection on the fragility of our earthly resources and our dependence on God. The nakedness of the Nile symbolizes the vulnerability of any civilization that turns away from the Creator.

sens: Cultivated plot of land in a garden, where flowers or plants grow
Strip of land where herbs, spices, or flowers are sown or planted
Place where a plant takes root and develops
H6170.detail:
1. The flowerbed is a defined plot in a garden, where flowers or plants are cultivated. In the Song of Songs, the beloved's cheeks are compared to a flowerbed of spices (Song of Songs 5:13), an image of beauty, sweetness, and fragrance.
2. It is also a strip of land where particular vegetation grows: fragrant herbs, flowers, or plants that have been sown or planted for cultivation. The beloved descends to the flowerbed of spices to rest and gather flowers (Song of Songs 6:2).
3. By extension, it is the soil where a plant takes root and from which it draws its life. Ezekiel describes the vine planted in the flowerbed, which extends its roots there and depends on it for survival (Ezekiel 17:7, 17:10): the flowerbed is its soil, its vital environment.
H6170.origine: The Hebrew word עֲרוּגָה comes from a root that means "to arrange" or "to set in order." It thus denotes an orderly arrangement of land or planting, a space that is organized and defined. It is a concrete term, related to agriculture and gardening, to evoke a regular arrangement of crops.
H6170.emploi: The word flowerbed appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, only in poetic contexts: twice in the Song of Songs and twice in the prophecy of Ezekiel. In the Song, it evokes delicate beauty and fragrance that captivate the senses. In Ezekiel, it represents the fertile soil where a plant can sink its roots and grow. It is a poetic and figurative term, never used to simply describe an everyday vegetable garden.
H6170.portee: This word invites us to see in earthly beauty an image of divine tenderness. It also shows that all spiritual life needs to take root somewhere, in a soil that nourishes: a place, a community, a Word to sink into in order to grow and bear fruit.

sens: Wild donkey of the Middle East, lighter and faster than the domestic donkey
H6171.detail: 1. The wild ass is a wild animal related to the domestic donkey, but smaller, sturdier, and much faster. It is a free creature that lives in the steppes and desert areas of the Middle East, without human servitude. In Job 39:8, the wild ass explores the mountains in search of pastures, embodying the absolute freedom that only God can give to His creatures.
H6171.origine: The Hebrew word עָרוֹד (arod) belongs to the family of words designating the donkey (such as עַיִר, ayir, and חֲמוֹר, hamor). The Aramaic has the closely related form עֲרָד (arad) with the same meaning. These words evoke the idea of a burden or draft animal, but the qualifier "wild" distinguishes it from domesticated beasts that man controls.
H6171.emploi: The word wild ass appears only once in the Bible, in Job 39:8. In this passage, God questions Job about the mysteries of creation by asking: "Who has let the wild ass go free?" It is an image of God's creative power and the independence He grants to His creatures. The wild ass symbolizes here what escapes human control and remains under divine dominion alone.
H6171.portee: This passage reminds the believer that God reigns over all living creation, including what man cannot tame or possess. By discovering that God provides for the freedom and needs of the wild ass, we learn to trust in divine providence for all beings, without exception.

sens: The state of the body without clothing, exposed without covering
The act of uncovering or showing another person's body without their consent
The intimate parts of the body, which should remain covered out of modesty
The absence of defense, vulnerability (in a figurative sense)
The shame and dishonor that result from it
Indecency, behavior contrary to morality
H6172.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: physical nudity, the body devoid of clothing. In Genesis 9:22, Ham sees the nakedness of his father Noah sleeping in his tent.

2. A very important meaning in the Law: "to uncover the nakedness" of a relative means to have sexual relations with her or to attempt to do so. This is the major prohibition in Leviticus 18, where the expression recurs constantly. For example: "None of you shall approach any of his relatives to uncover their nakedness" (Leviticus 18:6).

3. The parts of the body considered shameful and that should not be exposed — what is called pudenda. This is why the priest must wear trousers over his undergarments when going up to the altar (Exodus 28:42).

4. In a figurative sense: vulnerability, lack of defense. Isaiah threatens Babylon: "Your nakedness shall be uncovered" (Isaiah 47:3), meaning that it will be exposed without protection to the vengeance of the Lord.

5. The shame and dishonor that accompany this exposure — as when Jerusalem is compared to a woman whose nakedness is uncovered as she is dragged through the streets (Ezekiel 16:36-37).

6. Indecency or immorality: a "cause for divorce" can be an "indecency" (literally a "word of nakedness") in Deuteronomy 24:1.
H6172.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root (עֲרָה) that means "to be naked" or "to be exposed." It evokes the fundamental idea of what is not covered, of what lacks protection. The same root gives rise to other words for nakedness or vulnerability. In Aramaic, the parallel word (עַרְוָה) means "dishonor," which shows how closely the idea of nakedness is related to shame in the Semitic mindset.
H6172.emploi: The word appears 40 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in three contexts. First, the story of Noah in Genesis 9 where Ham sees his father's nakedness: this is a serious act of disrespect. Secondly and primarily, in the Law of Israel: Leviticus 18-20 prohibits "uncovering the nakedness" of various relatives (sister, sister-in-law, aunt, niece, etc.). This prohibition recurs constantly and establishes the rules of sexual impurity. Thirdly, among the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Hosea), "to uncover nakedness" becomes an image of judgment or dishonor inflicted on Jerusalem or the nations — it is the adulterous woman exposed in public, stripped of all dignity. In Deuteronomy 23:14, the word rather means indecency in a broad sense.
H6172.portee: This word reminds believers of the importance of respecting the body — their own and that of others — as a gift from God that deserves modesty and protection. The Law that uses it constantly shows that sexuality is not an indifferent matter, but is framed by just limits to preserve family and honor. When the prophets use it in a figurative sense (to uncover the nakedness of a nation), they teach that God's judgment removes all protection from those who oppose Him.

sens: The humiliation of a person before others
The shame, dishonor that affects someone
The absence of respect towards a superior or authority
H6173.detail:
1. The word first evokes public humiliation, like nakedness that exposes someone to the gaze of others — a situation where dignity is compromised. In Ezra 4:14, the king's servants say that it is not fitting for them to see the king being despised: they fear that he will be reduced to a shameful condition before his subjects.
2. Contempt also refers to the shame or dishonor that attaches to a person or group, a state of ignominy that destroys esteem.
3. It can finally mean the absence of respect, the affront made to someone who should be honored — here, towards royal authority.
H6173.origine: This Hebrew word evokes the image of nakedness, of what is uncovered and exposed to view. This is why it easily transitions from the physical sense (nakedness) to the moral sense (shame, dishonor, humiliation). The Hebrew root expresses the idea of being naked, without protection, from which the idea of being exposed to contempt naturally derives.
H6173.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 4:14. In this passage, the advisors of King Artaxerxes express their concern that the king would be exposed to the contempt of his subjects if the rebellious Jews are not punished. It is a term used to highlight the danger that an authority faces when it is allowed to be dishonored, and to justify a repressive action.
H6173.portee: This text reminds us that political order and respect for authority are important in God's eyes — not through blind servitude, but as a condition for stable communal life. However, the divine Word always places the respect of God above the respect of men.

sens: without clothing
devoid of covering or protection
exposed, uncovered
without resources or destitute
H6174.detail:
1. Without clothing on the body: the word describes the physical state of one who has no clothes. In Genesis 2:25, man and woman are naked in the Garden of Eden, unashamed, for they do not yet know sin. It is also the state of one who has been stripped, like the poor who are not clothed (Job 22:6).
2. Devoid of covering or protection: the word can refer to one who lacks shelter or covering against the cold. In Job 24:7, the unfortunate pass the night naked, without clothing or covering; in Isaiah 20:2-4, the prophet walks naked to symbolize the captives and exiles from Egypt and Ethiopia, humiliated and defenseless.
3. Exposed, uncovered, visible without obstacle: the abode of the dead is naked before God (Job 26:6), meaning that nothing can remain hidden there. It is also the sense of total vulnerability: the naked symbolizes one who cannot hide anything.
4. Without resources or destitute: Job says that he came out naked from his mother's womb and will return there naked (Job 1:21), which means that he came into the world with nothing and will take nothing away. This meaning evokes complete destitution, the loss of all possessions.
H6174.origine: The Hebrew word arom comes from a root that expresses the idea of uncovering, removing. It belongs to the same family as words that denote exposure, nakedness, the uncovered. In Greek, the corresponding word is gymnos (from which comes "gymnasium"), which has the same connotation: without clothes, without veil, manifest.
H6174.emploi: The word appears about 15 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom books and among the prophets. It first describes the original innocent state of man in Genesis 2:25. It then designates the destitution of the poor and captives: in Job, those who have no clothing or shelter suffer from the cold; in Isaiah, the nakedness of the exiles symbolizes the humiliation of Egypt. It can also express moral or spiritual nakedness: the abode of the dead is naked before God, everything there is uncovered and judged. Finally, Job uses it to express powerlessness in the face of death: one is born naked, one dies naked, devoid of all that one has acquired.
H6174.portee: This word reminds the reader that all physical or spiritual destitution is visible to God and that material wealth is temporary. It also invites compassion towards the naked, those who lack clothing and protection: the Word asks to clothe the naked (Isaiah 58:7), not only out of charity, but in recognition that we all came into this world naked and will return naked. For the believer, it is a call to humility and charity towards the most vulnerable.

sens: One who acts with calculation, dissimulation, or malice
One who thinks before acting and shows good sense
One who understands and anticipates dangers
H6175.detail:
1. The word primarily describes one who uses cunning, calculation, or deception: this is how the serpent is described in Genesis 3:1 as 'cunning' in its seduction of the woman, or how Job 5:12 speaks of the 'cunning' plans of men that the Lord frustrates. It is an intelligence turned towards dishonesty.
2. But it can also mean 'prudent' in a good sense: one who thinks before acting, who hides their knowledge rather than flaunting it. Proverbs 12:23 praises the 'prudent' man who conceals his knowledge, contrasting with the fool who proclaims his folly. It is a wisdom that manifests itself through restraint.
3. Finally, the word applies to one who foresees misfortunes and avoids them: Proverbs 22:3 says, 'The prudent man sees evil and hides himself,' while the fool rushes headlong. It is an intelligence that anticipates danger.
H6175.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of nakedness, absence of naivety, thus clarity of vision. Hence the image: one who is not 'naked' mentally, who has their eyes open. The same root produces other words related to sagacity and the absence of naivety in the Hebrew language.
H6175.emploi: This word appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in Proverbs (8 times). It carries within it a tension: in Genesis 3:1, it describes the evil cunning of the serpent; but among the wise of Israel, it designates the prudence that should be honored. In Proverbs, it regularly characterizes one who acts with discernment (12:16, 12:23, 13:16), who sees evil and avoids it (22:3, 27:12), always contrasting with the fool who rushes headlong. It is thus a sagacity that is morally neutral in itself: it can serve evil (the serpent) or good (the prudent man).
H6175.portee: This word helps the Christian understand an important biblical tension: vigilance and discernment are not flaws, but gifts to cultivate. Jesus himself will speak of being 'wise as serpents' (Matthew 10:16). Proverbs teaches us to see danger, to think before acting, to measure our words — this is the wisdom of God, not naivety. But this prudence must remain in the service of justice and righteousness, never in the service of deception.

sens: One who is stripped bare, devoid of everything
A barren and withered shrub of the desert, probably the juniper
State of desolation and abandonment
H6176.detail:
1. The word first designates one who is completely stripped, naked, without resources — a poor person reduced to misery. In Jeremiah 17:6, the man who turns away from God becomes 'like a miserable one in the desert,' an image of total nakedness, without protection or hope.
2. Concretely, it is a stunted and barren shrub of the desert, likely the juniper or cypress: a dry, useless plant, incapable of bearing fruit. The word associates the tree with the idea of being stripped bare — it gives nothing.
3. Biblically, the term evokes spiritual and physical desolation: one who turns away from God is like a dead shrub in the heart of the desert, uninhabitable and abandoned (Jeremiah 48:6).
H6176.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means 'to be naked, stripped.' Its basic image is that of something that has lost its covering, its wealth, its meaning — a being or a plant reduced to the essentials and to poverty. The desert shrub that bears this name illustrates the idea: a tree without abundant foliage, without fruit, exposed to the sun's scorching.
H6176.emploi: This word appears twice in the book of Jeremiah, always to describe a condition of extreme misfortune. In Jeremiah 17:6, it characterizes the man who abandons God and loses all blessing — he becomes barren like that desert shrub. In Jeremiah 48:6, it is a cry of warning: flee and become like a miserable one in the desert, that is, save your life at the cost of wandering and nakedness. The word thus carries a double burden: physical distress and separation from grace.
H6176.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of a serious spiritual truth: turning away from God leads to sterility and desolation, not only materially but existentially. Conversely, it invites one to seek in God the source of life and fruitfulness, so as not to become like that dead shrub in the desert.

sens: Ancient city located in Transjordan, on the lands of Ammon near the Jabbok
H6177G.detail: Aroër is a fortified city of the ancient Near East, located east of the Jordan in the region of Ammon. It was assigned to the tribe of Gad during the land distribution (Numbers 32:34) and served as a major geographical landmark marking the borders of the Israelite territory. The city has a notable military history: it was the starting point of Jephthah's victory over the Ammonites (Judges 11:33), and it appears as a stop during the census of the people under David (2 Samuel 24:5). In the time of the prophet Isaiah, it had become a desolate and abandoned place, given over to livestock and emptied of its inhabitants, symbolizing the ruin of Israel's enemy kingdoms (Isaiah 17:2).
H6177G.origine: The name Aroër means 'ruins' in Hebrew, reflecting the dilapidated state of this ancient fortress. This meaning was appropriate to the geography of the place, a border region exposed to conflicts and devastations. The word is formed from a root evoking desolation and the collapse of structures.
H6177G.emploi: Aroër appears six times in the Old Testament, always as a specific geographical name. It is first mentioned during the land distribution at the conquest (Numbers 32:34, Joshua 13:25), then in military and administrative accounts: Jephthah's victory (Judges 11:33), crossing the Jordan during David's census (2 Samuel 24:5), and habitation of tribes (1 Chronicles 5:8). The prophet Isaiah invokes it as a symbol of the final ruin of the Ammonite cities (Isaiah 17:2). Aroër served as a border marker delineating the territory of Israel to the east of the Jordan, and its evolution from inhabited fortress to abandoned city illustrates the fate of lands on the periphery of the kingdom.
H6177G.portee: Aroër reminds readers that the borders of God's people, even established by His will, had to be defended and experienced periods of prosperity and ruin. The repeated mention of Aroër as a landmark underscores the importance of obedience in the sharing and occupation of the promised inheritance. Its final abandonment in Isaiah 17 invites reflection on the vanity of human cities in the face of divine judgment.

sens: fortified city of Transjordan, on the banks of the Arnon
H6177H.detail: Aroër is a city located on the north bank of the Arnon stream, in the region of Transjordan. It marks the southern limit of the territory conquered by Israel under Moses: it is where the domain of the Amorite king Sihon begins before Israel takes it (Joshua 12:2). The city then becomes an important landmark for delineating the territories of the tribes of Reuben and Gad, always mentioned as the starting point when describing these borders (Deuteronomy 2:36; Joshua 13:9, 13:16). Its name means 'ruins,' which may evoke either a state of desolation or simply a city built on an ancient site.
H6177H.origine: The Hebrew name עֲרֹעֵר (Aroër) literally means 'ruins' or 'damages,' formed from a root evoking destruction or barrenness. This name perhaps reflects the aspect of the site or its ancient history.
H6177H.emploi: Aroër is mentioned nine times in the Hebrew Bible, always as a geographical landmark. It first appears in the accounts of the conquest under Moses (Deuteronomy 2:36; 3:12; 4:48) to mark the southern limit of Sihon's territory. It reappears in the description of the borders of Reuben and Gad (Joshua 12:2; 13:9; 13:16) as a permanent reference point for delineating these lands. In the time of the judges and kings, it retains this administrative importance: it is mentioned again in the time of Gideon (Judges 11:26) and the kings of Israel (2 Kings 10:33).
H6177H.portee: Aroër reminds us how God gave Israel concrete and precise lands, and how every geographical detail matters in His plan. The fact that the text constantly returns to this same landmark shows the importance of order and clarity in the promised inheritance for each tribe.

sens: City in the south of Judah
Place of refuge and distribution of spoils
H6177I.detail: Aroër is a city in the southern region of Judah. It is where David sends part of the spoils taken from the Amalekites after defeating them (1 Samuel 30:28). The name literally means "ruins," which may evoke a place once destroyed or a site with ancient remains.
H6177I.origine: The Hebrew name עֲרֹעֵר (aroër) means "ruins" or "debris." It describes the aspect of the place: a location marked by ancient ruins. This name also appears elsewhere in Israel, notably east of the Jordan, but here it designates a city in the south of Judah.
H6177I.emploi: Aroër appears only once in the Old Testament at this location. After his victory over the Amalekites who had burned Ziklag and taken captives, David distributes the spoils to several cities in the south of Judah, including Aroër (1 Samuel 30:28). This mention shows that David had relationships with the inhabitants of this region, and that the city was significant enough to receive its share of the spoils.
H6177I.portee: This passage reveals how David maintains ties with the cities of southern Judah and generously rewards them. It is a moment when David acknowledges the importance of the cities that, in one way or another, support his political and military agenda.

sens: That inspires great fear, horror, or disgust
That is wild, steep, inhospitable
H6178.detail:
1. Terrifying refers to what provokes fear or aversion. In Job 30:6, the terrifying valleys are those where the miserable and the outcasts of society take refuge, dark and dreadful places. The word evokes less wild beauty than an atmosphere of dread and threat.
2. In the same verse, these terrifying valleys are also described as steep ravines, rocky and abrupt terrains — places where nature itself appears hostile and dangerous. It is both the physical character of the terrain and the moral impression it produces.
H6178.origine: The Hebrew word arots comes from a root expressing fear and terror. It belongs to the family of Hebrew words that describe what troubles or overwhelms. The basic image is that of something that provokes an inner tremor, a reaction of fear in the face of a spectacle or a place that exceeds or threatens.
H6178.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 30:6. In this passage, Job describes the extreme sufferings of the unfortunate and outcasts who inhabit the most desolate and dreadful regions of the desert: terrifying valleys, dark caves, inhospitable rocks. The context is one of poverty and abandonment, and the adjective emphasizes the terrifying and repulsive nature of these makeshift refuges.
H6178.portee: This word reminds us that fear and horror can attach themselves to places and situations, but also that God does not despise those relegated to the most difficult places on earth. Job himself, although wealthy, will be reduced to distress, showing the vanity of earthly certainties.

sens: Son of Gad and progenitor of a tribe of Israel
H6179.detail: 1. Eri is one of the sons of Gad, one of the twelve sons of Jacob, named in Genesis 46:16 during the descent into Egypt. He thus belongs to the generation of the Hebrew people who enter Egypt under Joseph's leadership. His name means "vigilant" or "one who watches," a quality that may have characterized his temperament or role. In Numbers 26:16, we see that his descendants constitute the family of the Erites, one of the branches of the clan of Gad at the time of the census in the desert, after the exodus from Egypt.
H6179.origine: The name Eri (עֵרִי) literally means "vigilant" or "one who watches." It comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of watching, staying alert. Like many biblical character names, it describes a virtue or characteristic. His descendants are designated by the gentilice "Erites," formed according to the Hebrew custom that creates a family name from the patronym of the founder.
H6179.emploi: Eri appears only twice in the Bible. First in Genesis 46:16, where he is listed among the sons of Gad who descend into Egypt with Jacob. Then in Numbers 26:16, where after the exodus from Egypt and the stay in the desert, his name reappears in the role of founder of a family, the Erites, who are counted during the second census of Israel. These two mentions situate him at a pivotal moment in Israel's history: the descent into Egypt and the settlement of the land after the Exodus.

sens: descendants of the clan of Eri, son of Gad
H6180.detail: The Erites form a family group in Israel, consisting of all the descendants of Eri. Eri was one of the sons of Gad, himself a son of Jacob, and lived during the time of slavery in Egypt and the crossing of the desert. At the time of the census of the people of Israel in the desert (Numbers 26), the Erites appear as a family among the twelve tribes, listed alongside other clans of the same ancestor.
H6180.origine: The name Erites comes from the patronym Eri ("Eri"), which means "vigilant" or "one who watches." It follows the Hebrew custom of naming a family according to the name of its founding ancestor. Eri himself was the son of Gad, who was one of the twelve sons of Jacob and the founder of the tribe of Gad.
H6180.emploi: The Erites are mentioned only once in the Bible, during the census of the Israelites in the desert after the exodus from Egypt (Numbers 26:16). This census lists all the families of each tribe, and the Erites are included as one of the families of the tribe of Gad. No other details of their particular history are reported in the Scriptures.

sens: State of a person without clothing
Exposure or shameful deprivation
Absence of protection or defense
H6181.detail:
1. Nudity is primarily the physical state of a person devoid of clothing: in Ezekiel 16:7, the prophet describes a young woman who "was naked" at her birth, without any clothing. It is the image of the newborn or one who has nothing to cover themselves.
2. Nudity becomes a condition of shame and vulnerability: in Ezekiel 16:39 and 23:29, nudity is a punishment inflicted on Jerusalem — her clothing is taken away and she is "left naked," exposing her shame publicly. It is an act of contempt and humiliation.
3. Figuratively, nudity means exposure without protection, complete deprivation: in Habakkuk 3:9, "your bow is laid bare" means that the Lord's bow is uncovered, ready for action, with nothing to hide it.
H6181.origine: The Hebrew word עֶרְיָה (eryah) comes from the root עָרָה (arah), which means "to be naked, stripped." This root expresses the idea of exposure and discovery. It also forms the verb "to undress" and the adjective "naked." The Hebrew word concretely translates physical deprivation, but in the prophets, it acquires a moral and theological sense: nudity becomes a symbol of shame, defeat, and divine abandonment.
H6181.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, primarily in the writings of two prophets: Ezekiel mentions it four times to describe the nudity of Jerusalem as punishment (16:7, 16:22, 16:39, 23:29), depicting the city exposed to shame after its unfaithfulness. Micah uses it once (1:11) in a call to pass in nakedness and shame, announcing judgment. Habakkuk uses it once (3:9) to describe the Lord's bow laid bare — uncovered and ready to strike. The word thus remains concentrated in the prophetic language of judgment and exposure.
H6181.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that nudity — in the literal or figurative sense — is linked to vulnerability, loss of protection, and shame in the face of sin. It is a call to recognize that without the covering of God's grace, we are exposed and defenseless. Conversely, being clothed by God (with a robe of righteousness, to use the prophetic image) is an essential blessing and protection.

sens: Dough made by kneading flour with water
Portion of dough taken as an offering to the Lord
Firstfruits of bread, due to the priest or the Levite
H6182.detail:
1. Dough is the preparation obtained by mixing and kneading flour with water before baking — it is the raw material for bread. In Numbers 15:20, the Israelites are commanded to present "the firstfruits of your dough" to God, indicating that it refers to the dough prepared in each household.
2. This term primarily refers to the portion of dough that the owner must set aside and offer to the Lord. Numbers 15:20-21 organizes this obligation: with each batch, a part of the dough is separated as recognition of God's gift and the bread He provides.
3. By extension, it is one of the firstfruits due to the priests and Levites for their sustenance. Nehemiah 10:37 and Ezekiel 44:30 show that this offering of dough was a legal obligation that supported the priests and ensured their livelihood.
H6182.origine: The Hebrew word אֲרִיסָה comes from a root that evokes the idea of kneading or mixing. It is a concrete term: the dough that is kneaded by hand. The word only appears in passages related to the law of Leviticus and its reminders in later books.
H6182.emploi: This word appears 4 times, exclusively in legislative texts or in the reminder of these laws. Two occurrences are found in Numbers 15:20-21, where Moses prescribes to Israel to set aside the firstfruits of the dough as a perpetual offering; two others in Nehemiah 10:37 and Ezekiel 44:30, where this obligation is recalled as a duty towards the priests and Levites. The meaning remains constant: it is always the portion of dough that must be offered.
H6182.portee: This offering of dough reminds the believer that daily bread comes from God and that it must be acknowledged by offering the firstfruits — the best and first fruits of one's labor. It also teaches that the support of God's servants (priests and Levites) must be the responsibility of the entire community, as inscribed in the Law itself.

sens: The visible airspace above the earth, from which rain falls and storms come
The clouds and atmosphere that veil the day
The ensemble of visible elements: clouds, storm, darkness
H6183.detail: 1. Heaven refers to the space above the earth from which meteorological phenomena originate — rain, storm, darkness. In Isaiah 5:30, the prophet describes a day of judgment when "darkness will reign in heaven": it is the very image of heaven darkening, becoming a black and threatening veil. 2. This word depicts the atmosphere, not the infinite space, but what envelops and covers: the layer of clouds and vapors. The meaning oscillates between the visible vault and what it contains. 3. In the biblical context of misfortune, heaven expresses the feeling of oppression and judgment: when darkness reigns there, it is because God hides His face and misfortune approaches.
H6183.origine: The Hebrew word עָרִיף (aríph) comes from a root meaning "to flow" or "to rain." Heaven is thus first viewed as the source of the waters that fall from above. It is a concrete image: what we see up there is what descends and affects us — rain, wind, storms.
H6183.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 5:30. The prophet uses it to depict the covered and threatening sky on the day of divine judgment. It is a dramatic image: while the earth shows only darkness, heaven itself becomes dark, deepening the contrast between hope and anguish. Although rare, the word captures a very visual reality — that of a darkening sky — and gives the prophecy a poetic intensity.
H6183.portee: This verse reminds us that God's judgment is reflected in heaven itself: a darkness reigning in both worlds, earthly and heavenly, expresses the gravity of the moment and the invisibility of God. For the believer, the visible heaven is also a word from God — not seeing it means being separated from His light.

sens: One who exerts brutal and destructive force
One who inspires fear through power and authority
One who acts with tyranny and oppression
One who manifests formidable power
Impious, without respect for God
H6184.detail:
1. The word primarily describes a person who uses brutal force to dominate or destroy: it is the violent enemy who threatens (Job 6:23), the wicked who prospers in his strength (Psalms 37:35).
2. It also evokes impressive and terrifying power, which inspires dread: tyrants whose breath is as fearsome as a hurricane (Isaiah 25:4), or the powerful hero who instills fear in his adversaries (Jeremiah 20:11).
3. The violent is often a tyrant, a merciless oppressor: one who rules by terror and crushes the weak under his power.
4. The word can simply denote an imposing power, a remarkable force, without a defined moral connotation: a "force" or "might" (Proverbs 11:16).
5. Finally, the violent is frequently described as impious, one who rejects God and acts without fear of Him: the scoffer and the wicked who will be exterminated (Isaiah 29:20).
H6184.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to tremble" or "to fear." The starting image is that which evokes terror, which makes one tremble. From there arises the idea of what is terrible, powerful, formidable, then that of a tyrant or an oppressor who imposes fear. The family of the word also includes verbs evoking brute force, arrogance, and oppression.
H6184.emploi: This word appears about twenty times in wisdom and prophetic texts: Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. It almost always describes a person, never a thing. Sometimes it designates an enemy, an oppressor, a tyrant whom God fights or destroys (Isaiah 29:20: "the violent shall be no more"); sometimes it characterizes a powerful man whom the Lord triumphs over (Jeremiah 20:11). In Isaiah 25:3-5, the "tyrants" of the nations are opposed to the "weak" and "unfortunate" whom God protects. The word generally carries a negative moral tint: the violent refuses God and oppresses the small.
H6184.portee: This term reminds the reader that God does not turn a blind eye to oppression and brutality. It assures that tyrants, no matter how powerful they seem, will not last: the Lord is a refuge for the weak and a avenger for the oppressed. It is a word of hope for those who suffer injustice, and a warning for those who abuse their power.

sens: devoid of children, barren
deprived of descendants and inheritance
stricken by a curse or divine punishment
H6185.detail:
1. The word describes a person who has no children. This is Abram's state when he complains to God: "I go childless" (Genesis 15:2), meaning he will have no heir to perpetuate his name and receive his possessions.

2. Being childless means being deprived not only of descendants but of all that this represents in biblical life: inheritance, the continuity of the name, material security, and social honor. It is a situation of great precariousness.

3. The Law pronounces this condition as punishment against those who commit certain grave sins: men who violate sexual prohibitions "will die childless" (Leviticus 20:20-21). Similarly, Jeremiah announces to King Jehoiakim that he will be "deprived of children," meaning his descendants will not reign, sealing his disgrace.
H6185.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be naked" or "to be stripped." The absence of children is perceived as a nakedness, a total destitution: one is stripped of what constitutes the wealth of life. This term concretely translates the emptiness and isolation of one who has no descendants.
H6185.emploi: This word appears four times in the Bible, always to express a dramatic situation. For Abraham, it is a cry of distress in the face of the impossibility of having a natural heir (Genesis 15:2). In the purity code of Leviticus, it is the punishment promised to transgressors of sexual laws (Leviticus 20:20-21): those who commit incest or other grave violations will be condemned to remain childless, annihilating their posterity. Finally, the prophet Jeremiah uses it to describe the curse that strikes the wicked king Jehoiakim: although he is a man, none of his sons will sit on the throne of David (Jeremiah 22:30).
H6185.portee: This word reminds us that in the Old Testament, the absence of children is perceived as a tragedy and a curse. It embodies emptiness, a rupture with the future, the failure of the promise. But it also reveals the critical importance of faith: it is precisely in this state of apparent barrenness that Abraham believes in God's promise and becomes the father of a multitude (Genesis 15:4-6). The word invites us to meditate on how God can transform a situation of death into life, a human impossibility into divine wonder.

sens: Methodically place several things in good order
Prepare and arrange what will be presented or used
Organize fighters in battle formation
Set up an argument or position in a debate
Compare, put on the same level
H6186A.detail: 1. Arrange means to place objects in a thoughtful and organized order. This is the basic image: the lamps of the lampstand are arranged regularly (Leviticus 24:4), the wood for the sacrifice is arranged on the altar (Leviticus 1:7-8), and a table is set with its dishes in order (Proverbs 9:2). 2. Prepare goes further: it is not just about ordering, but making ready for use. One prepares the altar, one prepares their case by presenting it clearly before someone (Job 33:5). 3. Arrange for battle means to form an army in battle order, each group in its place for combat. This is a very frequent usage: the kings of Canaan arrange themselves against Abraham (Genesis 14:8), Israel and the Philistines form battle array against each other (1 Samuel 17:21), Joab arranges his troops against the Syrians (1 Chronicles 19:10). 4. Arranging one's case or words means to dispose them logically in a debate, presenting them in good argumentative order. 5. Compare or be comparable: the word can also mean to put in parallel, to measure the equality between two things.
H6186A.origine: The Hebrew verb עָרַךְ (arakh) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to put in order, align." The image is that of things arranged side by side according to a plan. The word is active and concrete: it describes an action of the one who organizes. In Hebrew, there is also the noun עֵרֶךְ (erekh, value or rank) that derives from it — which shows that arranging something gives it a place and value in an organized whole.
H6186A.emploi: The verb arakh appears 67 times in the Old Testament. It is first used in the context of worship: arranging the lamps of the lampstand, arranging the wood on the altar of burnt offerings, preparing the incense. It is a very frequent verb in Exodus and Leviticus to describe the tasks of worship. It is also massively used for battle formations: armies arrange themselves against each other, generals like Joab or David arrange their troops. It is also found in debates and trials: arranging one's case means presenting it in order. Job asks God to let him arrange his case before Him. In the Psalms, God "arranges" His table before the psalmist (Psalm 23:5) — an image of providential care. The verb can also express a comparison: comparing one thing to another or equating them.
H6186A.portee: This word reminds us that order is not superficial: to arrange something is to honor it and prepare it for its use. In worship, the methodical arrangement of elements expresses respect towards God. In battle, arranging in order means accepting to be part of an organized army. In prayer and debate, arranging one's words means saying them with clarity and strength. The word encourages us to see organization and preparation as serious and meaningful acts.

sens: Evaluate the value of something to officially set it
Determine the amount of a tax or contribution owed by someone
H6186B.detail:
1. Assess means to look at something and set its official value. This is the role of the priest in Leviticus 27: he examines an object consecrated to the Lord — a house, an animal — and evaluates its value according to its condition (good or bad), in order to determine the compensation due if the one who consecrated it wants to redeem it. The priest's assessment is final and binding on all (Leviticus 27:12).
2. Assess can also mean to set the amount of a tax that each person must pay. When Jehoiakim needs gold and silver for Pharaoh, he "assesses" the land — that is, he evaluates the resources of each Israelite and determines the share that each must contribute (2 Kings 23:35).
H6186B.origine: The Hebrew root עָרַךְ (arakh) evokes the idea of arranging, ordering, setting up. It describes an action of structuring and calculating, as when one "arranges" words in a speech or objects in order. The meaning of "assess" comes from this notion: to evaluate is to put in order the criteria and calculate the value. The Hiphil (conjugated form used here) reinforces the idea of a directed action: the one who assesses imposes their judgment.
H6186B.emploi: The verb עָרַךְ appears 4 times in the Bible, always in the Hiphil form (which gives the meaning of "assess" or "tax"). Three occurrences are found in Leviticus 27:8, 12, and 14 in the context of voluntary consecrations: the Lord allows an Israelite to redeem their vow, but the priest must assess the value of what has been vowed. This assessment is decisive and binding (Leviticus 27:12: "one will rely on the priest's assessment"). The fourth occurrence, in 2 Kings 23:35, is outside this religious context: Jehoiakim "assesses" the land to raise the gold and silver required by Pharaoh. In the first three cases, the word emphasizes the justice and precision of judgment; in the last, it highlights the exercise of fiscal power.
H6186B.portee: This word reminds us that the value of things consecrated to God does not depend on our feelings or desires, but on an objective and fair evaluation. Even in the sacred realm, God establishes clear criteria and authorized mediators (the priest) to apply the Law. It also teaches us that a tax imposition must be fair and proportionate to each person's resources, not arbitrary.

sens: Regular arrangement, orderly disposition
Assessment of the value of a person or thing
Price set according to this assessment
H6187.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a regular and organized arrangement: things arranged in good order, set in place. Thus, in Exodus 40:4, the table is set and the lamps of the lampstand are arranged: everything is put in "order".
2. The meaning extends to the evaluation itself, the action of estimating the value of someone or something. Leviticus 27:12 speaks of the priest who "will make the estimation" of an object "according to whether it is good or bad".
3. The word also refers to the price or value set by this evaluation. In Leviticus 27:5, it reads: "your estimation shall be twenty shekels for a male, and ten shekels for a female" — this is the amount of money assigned to each person according to their age and gender.
H6187.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to arrange" or "to order." It evokes the idea of putting in rows, arranging correctly. Its religious use in Leviticus reflects the biblical concern for precision and regularity: God establishes just and orderly estimation rules for people or goods consecrated to the Temple.
H6187.emploi: This word appears about 29 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Leviticus. It is concentrated in Leviticus 27, the chapter on vows and consecrations, where the value of a person, an animal, or property offered to the Lord is assessed. In Exodus 40:4, it means rather "order" or "arrangement." In the passages of Leviticus 5 and 27, the priest makes the estimation according to established rules: age and gender for people (Leviticus 27:3-7), the condition of the property for fields (Leviticus 27:16-18). The result is always expressed in sanctuary shekels (Leviticus 27:25). This system shows how the Law frames voluntary gifts with wisdom and fairness.
H6187.portee: This word reminds the believer that God establishes order and sets values according to His justice. There is no arbitrariness in the gifts consecrated to God: everything is measured, regular, fair. It teaches that our commitment to God must also be thoughtful and orderly: neither haste nor laxity, but a deliberate and responsible consecration.

sens: Treat something as impure or unavailable, marking it with a religious prohibition
Leave something in its raw or unexploited state
Expose oneself to shame or dishonor by uncovering oneself
H6188.detail:
1. In Leviticus 19:23, the word refers to the act of considering the fruits of a newly planted tree as "uncircumcised," meaning impure or forbidden for consumption for three years. The image of circumcision, a sign of covenant, is applied to the fruits: as long as a fruit is not "circumcised" (that is, consecrated and made available after the ritual period), it remains taboo, out of use.
2. The figurative meaning suggests leaving something fallow or unharvested, like land or fruits that are not picked. It is a way of saying that something remains in its initial state, untransformed or unused.
3. In Habakkuk 2:16, "uncover yourself" carries a sense of shame: the word refers to ignominious exposure, the act of being found naked or stripped of dignity. It is the opposite of the protection that the covenant provides: to uncover oneself is to lose one's honorable covering and fall into disgrace.
H6188.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root that evokes circumcision and everything that is uncircumcised. The basic idea is that of the uncircumcised, that which has not undergone the ritual mark of the covenant. In Hebrew thought, what is "uncircumcised" is profane, outside the sacred order established by God. The word is used first literally (the uncircumcised peoples), then figuratively extends to anything that is impure, unavailable, or dishonored.
H6188.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Leviticus 19:23, it is a ritual and agricultural prescription: the fruits of the first three years are "considered uncircumcised" and thus untouchable, consecrated to the Lord. In Habakkuk 2:16, the context is prophetic and threatening: it is a threat from God against Babylon, which will be forced to "uncover itself" in shame, to suffer public disgrace. The word shifts from the cultic and agricultural domain to the realm of cursing and judgment.
H6188.portee: For the believer, these two uses remind us that the covenant with God creates sacred distinctions: certain things, certain times, certain acts are marked by the presence of God and require respect and consecration. The first image (the uncircumcised fruits) teaches patience and obedience to the rhythms that God sets. The second (the shameful uncovering) warns that rejecting the covenant leads to public ruin and dishonor. It is an invitation to remain within God's order rather than rebel against Him.

sens: Who has not undergone circumcision, who retains his foreskin
Who does not belong to God's covenant with Israel
Who is outside the people of God, foreign or enemy
Whose heart is closed to God, rebellious and unbelieving
H6189.detail:
1. An uncircumcised person is literally a man who has not had his foreskin removed by circumcision. God commanded Abraham and his descendants to be circumcised as a sign of the covenant; one who refuses or neglects this practice is uncircumcised (Genesis 17:14). It is primarily a physical fact.
2. The word thus refers to one who is not part of the people of Israel or who refuses to join it. An uncircumcised person is excluded from the Passover (Exodus 12:48) and from the holy communion of Israel. It is a religious and communal boundary.
3. By extension, "uncircumcised" becomes a term to designate enemies and pagan peoples, notably the Philistines. David calls Goliath "this uncircumcised one" to emphasize that he is an enemy of the living God (1 Samuel 17:26). The word then expresses contempt or separation.
4. Figuratively, God speaks of an "uncircumcised" heart or ear to describe spiritual resistance: a soul closed to His word, a people that refuses to listen despite judgment (Leviticus 26:41; Jeremiah 6:10). It is the image of inner hardness.
H6189.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to strip away" or "to expose." The uncircumcised is one who has not had his foreskin removed. In Hebrew, circumcision is one of the strongest marks of the covenant with God, established as early as Abraham. Because it is so central to Israel's identity, the word "uncircumcised" eventually comes to designate not only a physical state but also a spiritual condition: one who is separated from God or who refuses His covenant.
H6189.emploi: The word appears 32 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly to qualify the enemies of Israel, particularly the Philistines. In the literal sense, it describes one who has not been circumcised (Genesis 17:14; Exodus 12:48; Joshua 5:7). But very quickly, it takes on a broader meaning: it designates foreign peoples (Ezekiel 32:19-32, which lists the uncircumcised nations that have descended to the realm of the dead). Finally, it becomes a spiritual image to speak of rejection of God: an uncircumcised ear is an ear that refuses to hear (Jeremiah 6:10), an uncircumcised heart is a hardened heart (Leviticus 26:41). This progression from the concrete to the spiritual shows how the Bible uses the language of the covenant to express faithfulness or rebellion against God.
H6189.portee: The word "uncircumcised" reminds us that the covenant with God is not automatic: it requires a visible commitment, a voluntary separation for Him. Spiritually, it warns the believer against hardness of heart and stubbornness: to be "uncircumcised of heart" is to refuse the transformative work of God. Under the New Covenant, the circumcision of the heart (not that of the flesh) becomes central (Romans 2:28-29), and this word invites us to examine our inner obedience to God, beyond appearances.

sens: The skin that covers the tip of the male member
State of one who has not undergone circumcision
Symbol of impurity or separation from God
Absence of consecration to God's covenant
H6190G.detail:
1. The foreskin is literally the skin covering the tip of the male member in men. It is a simple physical reality that any reader can understand.

2. The state of being uncircumcised, one who retains his foreskin, refers to the man who has not received circumcision — the act of removing this skin that marked the covenant with God. At Gilgal, Joshua circumcises all the men who grew up in the desert: the text refers to "Gilgal of the foreskins" (Joshua 5:3), for it is there that what marked them as outsiders disappears.

3. In biblical thought, the foreskin becomes an image of everything that separates from God: impurity, rebellion, a hardened heart. Jeremiah speaks of uncircumcised ears, Stephen of a people with uncircumcised hearts and ears — not by the body, but by the soul closed to God.

4. Beyond the medical act, the absence of circumcision expresses the absence of a covenant relationship with the God of Israel, a rupture in the covenant of grace.
H6190G.origine: The Hebrew word עׇרְלָה (orlah) comes from a root that denotes the idea of covering or veil. In biblical language, it initially retains its concrete physical meaning, then enriches itself with a spiritual and moral sense: everything that remains veiled, hidden, or separated from God. The word is also used for the fruits of the first three years of a tree, which were considered non-consecrated — even an image of a reality not yet offered to God.
H6190G.emploi: The word orlah appears only once in the provided usages: Joshua 5:3, where it refers to the foreskin of the Israelites who, born in the desert, had not been circumcised. The context is decisive: it is the moment when Joshua restores the covenant, marking the entry into the Promised Land through this foundational rite. Elsewhere in the Old Testament, the word also applies to the forbidden fruits of young trees, showing how the Bible uses this image of uncircumcision for everything that has not yet received consecration to God.
H6190G.portee: This word reminds the believer that God's covenant is not automatic, but requires a voluntary and embodied consecration — physical circumcision prefigured the circumcision of the heart. To see one's foreskin removed was to acknowledge: I belong to God, I do not withhold myself from Him. For the Christian reader, this clarifies why Paul insists: true circumcision is that of the heart, by the Spirit (Romans 2:29). The external sign is only valuable when carried by the inner offering.

sens: Part of the skin of the male member, removed by circumcision
One who has not been circumcised, the uncircumcised
State or character of that which has not been consecrated or has not reached maturity
Closed heart, hardened, impermeable to God
H6190H.detail:
1. The foreskin is the skin that covers the glans of the male member in men. It is the part that the Hebrews would remove during circumcision, a central religious and identity act for Israel. Exodus 4:25 shows this concretely: Zipporah cuts off her son's foreskin with a sharp stone.
2. By metonymy, "uncircumcised" refers to any man who has not undergone this circumcision — notably the Philistines and other pagan peoples who do not belong to the covenant of Israel. Genesis 34:14 testifies to this: giving the sister to an "uncircumcised" man was a disgrace, a violation of the identity of the people.
3. Circumcision, being practiced only on the eighth day after birth (Leviticus 12:3), also served to mark consecration or entry into covenant. By extension, that which does not have this mark is "uncircumcised" in the sense that it is not yet mature or available: the fruits of a tree during three years are considered "uncircumcised" (Leviticus 19:23), meaning they are forbidden for consumption.
4. Finally, the word becomes a spiritual image among the prophets: "circumcise your heart" (Deuteronomy 10:16) means to remove hardness and pride to make it docile to God. An "uncircumcised heart" is a closed heart, rebellious to the divine voice.
H6190H.origine: The Hebrew word עׇרְלָה comes from a root that denotes skin or covering. In Hebrew, circumcision (ברִית־מִילָה, "covenant of circumcision") was the visible sign of belonging to the people of Israel and of the covenant with God. The foreskin thus represented what must be removed to become a member of this chosen people. The usage of the word gradually extends from the physical and literal meaning to the figurative and spiritual sense, particularly in prophetic preaching.
H6190H.emploi: The word appears 15 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Torah (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy) and in historical narratives (Samuel). Initially concrete and legal — Genesis 17:11-25 establishes circumcision as the sign of the Abrahamic covenant — it gradually becomes an identity marker. David's warriors bring Philistine foreskins to Saul (1 Samuel 18:25, 18:27) as proof of victory over the enemies of the people. The word also applies metaphorically to immaterial realities: the "uncircumcised" fruits of the first three years (Leviticus 19:23) must not be eaten, as they have not reached their consecration. Finally, the prophets use it to criticize the absence of spiritual repentance: an "uncircumcised heart" (Jeremiah 4:4, 9:25) is a conscience that refuses to submit to God, despite physical circumcision.
H6190H.portee: This word reveals the fundamental tension between the external sign and the internal reality of faith. The circumcision of the foreskin was the visible seal of the covenant with God, but the prophets warned that the circumcised flesh was of no value without a transformed heart. For today's believer, this word invites examination of whether one only bears the appearances of faith or has truly allowed God to remove the hardness of their heart. The New Testament will take up this image, applying it to baptism and the conversion of the heart.

sens: To be subtle, sly, crafty in one's actions or thoughts
To act with prudence and discernment
To resort to tricks or detours to achieve a goal
H6191.detail:
1. To be cunning means to show subtlety and malice — to act in secret, with ulterior motives. David describes Goliath as "strong and cunning" (1 Samuel 23:22), suggesting that a cunning man is dangerous because he calculates his moves.
