The enemies of Israel form "cunning plans" against the people of God (Psalms 83:4): this is a hostile, malicious cunning.
2. However, cunning can also refer to wise prudence and discernment — a form of practical wisdom. In Proverbs 15:5, the one who "acts with prudence" shows that he listens to rebuke: this is a positive cunning, that of the man who knows how to correct himself. In Proverbs 19:25, the scoffer struck "will become wise": this is a cunning of correction that produces wisdom.
3. Cunning also means to resort to clever tricks or detours. Job 5:13 speaks of the "wise caught in their own cunning": the complicated plans of men end up trapping them. This is cunning as twisted calculation, as machination.
H6191.origine: The Hebrew verb עָרֹם (a.ram) fundamentally expresses the idea of subtlety, hidden malice, but also of clear-sighted prudence — two facets of the same reality: intelligence that calculates in silence. This duality is found in the Hebrew Bible, where cunning can be the trait of the wise who sees clearly, or of the wicked who plots. The word belongs to a semantic field close to sagacity and clever discernment.
H6191.emploi: The verb appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always as a noun or adjective ("cunning", "crafty"). It first describes the dangerous enemy: David seeks to know Goliath's movements because he is cunning (1 Samuel 23:22). It also characterizes the malicious plans of God's adversaries: the enemies of Israel deliberate with cunning (Psalms 83:4), and the wise of men are caught in their own game (Job 5:13). But cunning also receives a positive value in Proverbs: it becomes prudence, discernment, the ability to listen and learn. It is the sign of one who understands the lesson and becomes wise.
H6191.portee: Cunning reminds us that the Bible does not sharply oppose good and evil, naivety and intelligence. God Himself can use cunning — that of the wise who confounds the plans of the wicked. For the believer, this word invites discernment: cunning can be the weapon of God's enemies, but it can also be the clear-sighted wisdom of one who listens to God and avoids traps. It is a lesson on vigilant observation and wise listening.

sens: To accumulate in heaps, to pile up
To rise up, to form a barrier
(Figuratively) The effect of the divine breath that lifts and organizes
H6192.detail:
1. The word describes the action of waters that accumulate and pile up on top of each other, forming heaps. It is the concrete image of things gathering, rising in a pile. At the Red Sea (Exodus 15:8), this is what happens to the waters under the breath of God: they heap up.
2. This verb suggests less a simple piling up than an organization, a structure: the heaped waters rise up, forming a solid wall. The accumulation here creates something vertical and stable.
3. The text uses this word to express the power of the divine breath (the "nostrils" of the Lord). It is not a chaotic piling up, but the effect of a will that shapes the elements and creates the order of the miracle.
H6192.origine: The Hebrew root עָרַם comes from a very ancient image: that of piling up, of heaping. The Niphal (passive or reflexive form in Hebrew) expresses here the idea that the waters heap up by themselves, as under an external force. The verb belongs to the family of words that express accumulation and the construction of visible structures.
H6192.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Exodus 15:8, in the Song of the Sea. It is the moment when Moses celebrates the crossing of the Jordan and the victory of the Lord over the waters of the Red Sea. The context is that of a miracle of deliverance: the waters, at the breath of God, heap up and rise like a wall, while the Israelites cross on dry ground. It is a moment of admiration before divine power. The unique use of this verb makes it a rare and solemn term, reserved for this climactic moment in the Exodus narrative.
H6192.portee: This word reveals how nature itself obeys God and becomes an instrument of His will. For the reader, it shows that the "breath" (or Spirit) of the Lord is not abstract: it acts concretely, it organizes and transforms creation. This encourages the believer to recognize in the signs of the world the trace of divine power and its ability to reorganize our lives according to His plan.

sens: accumulation of piled things
a mound, a heap of material
a sheaf of grain
accumulation as a reserve or provision
H6194.detail:
1. The most common meaning: a pile of objects or materials accumulated in one place. Ruth 3:7 shows Boaz sleeping "at the end of a heap of sheaves", that is, near a harvest gathered in the field.
2. By extension, a pile of dust or debris. Nehemiah 4:2 speaks of "mounds of dust" where the old stones of Jerusalem rested, evoking the accumulated ruins.
3. A sheaf of grain, that is, a bundle of stalks tied together after the harvest. This is a particular meaning of the word, applied to sheaves of wheat or barley.
4. In the context of management, the word refers to the accumulation of goods or provisions for storage. In 2 Chronicles 31:6-9, the priests and Levites create "heaps" by collecting the offerings, and then Hezekiah comes to "see the heaps" to check the sacred reserves.
H6194.origine: The Hebrew word עֲרֵמָה (aremah) derives from a root expressing the idea of gathering or accumulating. It is related to the verb "to pile up", and the word evokes the concrete action of putting together several things until forming a mound. The basic image is that of a visible and tangible accumulation, whether of harvest, dust, or provisions.
H6194.emploi: The word appears about 10 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical and poetic narratives. It is used to describe the sheaves of harvest (Ruth 3:7), the reserves of tithes and offerings in the temple (2 Chronicles 31:6-9), and the heaps of ruins or dust (Nehemiah 4:2). In each context, it retains its fundamental meaning of material accumulation, but its nuance varies depending on whether it concerns accumulated wealth (religious or economic priority), destruction (ruins), or simply harvested crops. The word also appears in biblical poetry (Song of Songs 7:3) for figurative comparisons.
H6194.portee: This word invites the reader to see how God blesses and accumulates provisions for His people. In 2 Chronicles 31, the "heaps" of offerings manifest the generosity of the people and divine providence: Hezekiah and the leaders "blessed the Lord" as they contemplated these reserves. It is also a reminder that material wealth is a gift to be managed with wisdom and gratitude.

sens: Ability to understand hidden things, to see beyond appearances
Wise prudence, sagacity in judgment
Cunning, stratagem used to deceive or circumvent an obstacle
H6195.detail:
1. Discernment is the ability to perceive what is not obvious, to grasp the hidden dimensions of a situation. Wisdom itself, in Proverbs 8:12, states: "I, wisdom, dwell with discernment" — this word thus denotes a subtle intelligence, capable of untangling the true from the false.
2. This discernment can be virtuous: the wise prudence that helps a young man acquire "knowledge and discretion" (Proverbs 1:4), a wise way of judging and acting.
3. But the same word also denotes cunning, even deception: when the Gibeonites "acted with cunning" (Joshua 9:4), using old sacks and worn-out wineskins to pass themselves off as travelers from afar, or when a murderer acts "by employing cunning to kill him" (Exodus 21:14). It is the twisted skill used in the service of lies.
H6195.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be bare, stripped, exposed." It first denotes what is laid bare, uncovered, and then by extension what uncovers or reveals hidden things — hence the penetrating intelligence, sagacity. The word can thus slide from the good side (discernment) to the bad (malicious cunning), depending on whether it is used to seek truth or to deceive.
H6195.emploi: The word appears five times in biblical Hebrew, almost always in Proverbs and historical narratives. In Proverbs (1:4; 8:5; 8:12), it is a gift of wisdom, a quality of one who reflects and understands deeply. In the narratives (Exodus 21:14; Joshua 9:4), it describes the skill to devise a hidden plan: the criminal who kills with calculation, or the enemy who feigns to deceive. The context alone indicates whether it is a virtue or a vice.
H6195.portee: This word teaches that intelligence is not neutral: it can serve wisdom and justice, or become malicious cunning. The young Christian must seek discernment in the noble sense — this insightful penetration of good and evil — while guarding against deceptive cunning. It is a call to cultivate a humble and righteous intelligence.

sens: Large tree with broad leaves and naturally peeling bark
Wood from this tree, used for its properties
Majestic tree symbolizing strength and beauty
H6196.detail:
1. The plane tree is a large tree recognizable by its bark that peels off in plates, revealing the white wood underneath — this is what Jacob exploits in Genesis 30:37, where he peels the branches to expose the white of the bark, creating white and speckled strips intended to impress the livestock.
2. The wood of the plane tree, hard and durable, was valued for its practical uses and was associated with wealth and solidity.
3. In Ezekiel 31:8, the plane tree is among the majestic trees of God's garden, alongside cedars and cypresses, symbolizing impressive natural beauty and grandeur that only God can surpass.
H6196.origine: The Hebrew word עַרְמוֹן (armon) specifically refers to the oriental plane tree, a common tree in the Middle East and Mediterranean. Its characteristic image is that of a tree whose bark peels, revealing the white of the soft wood underneath — a striking feature that explains its symbolic role in Jacob's story.
H6196.emploi: The word plane tree appears twice in the Bible. In Genesis 30:37, Jacob uses peeled branches of the plane tree for a stratagem aimed at influencing the reproduction of the livestock: he creates visible white strips that recall the natural effect of the peeling bark. In Ezekiel 31:8, the plane tree is invoked as one of the most beautiful trees in God's garden, alongside the cedars of Lebanon and cypresses, to illustrate the unmatched majesty of the king of Egypt before his fall. In both cases, it represents something remarkable and notable.
H6196.portee: The plane tree reminds us that God's creation abounds in visible splendor: its majestic trees, striking details — like the bark that reveals the white — testify to divine wisdom and beauty. For Jacob, it also illustrates how God can use ordinary and observable things to fulfill His promises.

sens: Son of Shuthelah, descendant of Ephraim
H6197.detail: Éran is a man of the tribe of Ephraim, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Shuthelah and belongs to the genealogy of Ephraim, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. His descendants formed the clan of the Eranites, as indicated in Numbers 26:36 during the census in the wilderness: "the sons of Shuthelah: from Éran came the family of the Eranites." This census occurs at the end of the forty years of wandering in the wilderness, before entering the Promised Land.
H6197.origine: The name Éran means "the vigilant one" or "watchman," evoking the image of a watchful person. He belongs to the genealogy of Ephraim, son of Joseph. His name has given rise to the gentilé Eranite (עֵרָנִי), which designates the members of the clan descended from him.
H6197.emploi: Éran appears only once in the Scriptures, in Numbers 26:36. This mention occurs during the second census of the Israelites in the wilderness, after the first generation of the exodus. It is a genealogical document that lists the clans and their leaders, in preparation for the division of the Promised Land. Éran is identified there as the son of Shuthelah and the founding ancestor of the clan of the Eranites.

sens: descendants of Éran, son d'Éphraïm
H6198.detail: The Eranites are the members of the family clan descended from Éran, son of Shuthelah and grandson of Ephraim. This group is mentioned in the census of Israel in the wilderness, when Moses counts the tribes to prepare for the conquest of Canaan (Numbers 26:36). Like all the tribal groups listed in this passage, the Eranites form an organized family unit within the tribe of Ephraim, heir to the promises made to the patriarchs.
H6198.origine: The name comes from the ancestor Éran (עֵרָן), whose primitive meaning is "watchman" or "guardian." Éran was the son of Shuthelah and belonged to the tribe of Ephraim. The grammatical suffix transforms the name of the father into a clan name: "Eranites" designates all those who descend from this Éran. The genealogy places this family in the period of Egypt and the wilderness.
H6198.emploi: The Eranites are mentioned only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:36, during the second census of the Israelites in the wilderness, near the plains of Moab. At this time, Moses and Eleazar establish the role of each clan in view of the division of the promised land. The enumeration of the Eranites among the descendants of Shuthelah affirms their status as a legitimate tribal group and their right to a share of the inheritance in Canaan.
H6198.portee: The mention of the Eranites reminds us that God wants each of His children to be known by name and recognized in the community. Even a small clan, mentioned only once, has its place in God's plan and receives its promised inheritance. For the reader, it is an assurance that no one is forgotten before God, however small their number may be.

sens: Devoid of everything, reduced to extreme poverty
One who is despised or abandoned by men
One who cries out to God in distress
H6199.detail:
1. The word describes someone who is so poor and destitute that they have lost almost everything — their possessions, their dignity, sometimes even hope. It is the person at the bottom of the social ladder, without resources or protection (Psalms 102:18).
2. To be miserable also means to be ignored or despised by the world: the powerful do not notice them, the rich disdain them. It is a solitude and humiliation added to material poverty.
3. But in the Bible, misery opens the eyes: the miserable cries out to God, they pray, they confess their need. That is why God "does not despise" the prayer of the miserable (Psalms 102:18) — He listens where men reject them.
H6199.origine: The Hebrew word עָרוּר comes from a root that literally means "stripped, naked." The image is of a person from whom layer after layer has been removed — their clothing, their possessions, their pride. It is a rare word, found little in the Old Testament, and this rarity itself underscores the extreme nature of this condition.
H6199.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalm 102:18. It describes one who addresses their prayer to God in extreme destitution. The context of Psalm 102 is one of poignant cries: the author expresses their physical suffering, their solitude, their feeling of being forgotten. It is in this context that the word "miserable" takes on its full force: it denotes not only material state but the total humiliation of one who has nowhere to go but to God.
H6199.portee: This word teaches the reader that God sees those whom society forgets. It affirms that the poor, the rejected, the one who feels alone, has an audience with the eternal God. It is a word of hope for anyone going through trials: your prayer is not lost, your misery is not invisible to God.
